content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

The Chain Theater’s Program 13 is part of its series of 24 Programs of one-act plays that support both new writers and actors of theater. Simple sets and a cacophony of stories over several weeks. Each group of one acts, some 4 a night, some 3, and some 5, depending on length, are presented on The Chain’s 36th Street stage.

It is giving, gracious, and formidable to present so many shows over several weeks. Scheduling and creating evenings with a huge collection of 94 new pieces alone is an achievement. And so, thank you to The Chain for this gift to so many playwrights, actors, and directors.

It also means that performances are not always balanced. Each evening can have one good piece, followed by confusion, followed by excellence, and so on. And that is the chance you take, as once again I must state that The Chain is open to engaging audiences in new pieces and writers. Bravo Chain.

Program 13 is an imbalance of stories and production value. The limitations were in the volume and clarity of the performers. Some of the performers were speaking below everyday volume, so the story they were trying to tell was lost. We, the audience, became so quiet, straining to make out what was being said, and unfortunately, we remained lost. Thus, the storyline was lost to us. When unable to create interesting, intriguing sets with the time limit and space, you must then rely on the performers and the words spoken to move the story forward more than ever. With nothing to hang onto, it leaves the audience in limbo.

The evening consisted of four one-act plays: Doors are a Hammers Best Friend by Jociel Tambone, FREE SEX! by Hassan Sharif, Hair Salon and Sam by Linda Herskovic, and One Night by A. Dean Bell. These shows all have merit in the stories and the characters, but the production left us hanging again and again. The laissez-faire of some of the performers left the words falling and not floating, definitely not connecting. Actors practically whispering meant stories could not be followed because we, the audience, could not hear them. The exceptions to the evening FREE SEX! by Hassan Sharif set in a prison, and “Hair Salon Sam” by Linda Herskovic, as you can imagine, set in a hair salon, are both stories of people desperate and trying to connect. The actors gave it their all, and so we, the audience, laughed and listened. “One Night” has as a very plausible and interesting take on getting so drunk that you are not sure if you committed a rape. The ending scene is powerful, and thus, I encourage the writer to go deeper with that. The two leads together wondering what happened, one a perpetrator and the other the victim, were enthralling. “Doors are a Hammers Best Friend” is a terrific concept – roommates stuck in their apartment because the front door won’t open – but this one in particular was hard to follow, and only at the end did we understand the relationship of the third person in the room, and by then it was too late.

I do want to point out the respect and importance of the role of the audience and staying for the entire evening to support not only the one act you particularly came to see but all of the pieces in the evening.

And I want to thank The Chain again for its commitment and support, its time and dedication, to writers, actors, and directors, giving them a chance to test their wings.

“Doors are a Hammers Best friend” by Jociel Tambone and Directed by Nicole Ulloa   With: Daisy Duarte, Kevin Guaman and Stiles Ramirez

“FREE SEX!!” by Hassan Sharif and Directed by France Jones  With: Carson Thomas, Daniel Baesler, Xavier Jefferson, Jameal Bailey, Mia Fritz, and Adelia Castillo

“Hair Salon and Sam” by Linda Herskovic and Directed by Dave Bobb  With: Lily Potarf, MC Crosby, and Lauren Snyder

“One Night” written and directed by A. Dean Bell  With: Sasha Crews,  Krystal Ejesieme, Scott Bausemer, and Samuel Keran

The Chain Theatre 312 West 36 Street, Floors 3 & 4, New York, NY 10018

content.rendered:
By Vahni Kurra

In Jiggs Burgess’ Wounded, presented by SoHo Playhouse, the grief and rage of three people in a small, Texas town explode in a show that pulls no punches. Having won the 2024 SoHo Playhouse International Fringe Encore Theater Series Overall Excellence Award, Wounded comes to its Off Broadway run under the direction of Del Shores, acclaimed writer, director, and producer.

Katie (Kristen McCullough) is the beleaguered mother of Elizabeth, her thirteen year old daughter who was struck by a car at a young age and completely paralyzed. In one of their many outings to the park, Katie encounters Carrol (Craig Taggart), an older gay man with a luxurious fashion sense and a voice that’s a cross between Dolly Parton and Julia Child. He is also a nosy gossip who immediately annoys Katie. While she is guarded and high strung, Carrol projects a molasses-like ease, punctuated by high-pitched giggles at his own jokes. McCullough and Taggart deliver energized comedic performances with a particularly Southern, small town bent— throwing around “bless her heart”s and insults coated in politeness. They move between catty jibes and honest reflections on grief seamlessly, like a waltz between two compatible dancers. Taggart’s larger-than-life performance is magnificent, elevating every joke and bringing unexpected softness to sincere moments, and McCullough’s earnestness pulls at the heartstrings. Initially, I questioned the choice to represent Elizabeth, whom Katie affectionately calls “Sparrow,” as a doll in a wheelchair rather than having an actress. I wonder what the audience might have gained from being faced with the reality of a living, breathing person in this role who must remain on stage, in the same spotlight as her mother, and yet never be able to participate in a conversation that is largely about her. But this is not Elizabeth’s story. It’s Katie’s, and as much as she tries to treat her daughter as an autonomous person, it becomes clear that she also sees her as a broken thing to care for. Wounded doesn’t shy away from these morally gray areas, instead choosing to show how victims of tragedy can spread their misery and hurt to others.

We also see how empathy can sometimes be easier when we don’t know someone very well; when we don’t know the skeletons they keep in their closets. While Carrol comes across as a compassionate jester in the first act with Katie, we see a new side of him around Robert (Shaw Jones), a high school classmate and ex-con whom Carrol had an unrequited crush on. Jones looks the part of a former Texan homecoming king, and his immediate charm as Robert initially conceals the more sinister aspects of his character. If the first act was a waltz, the scenes between Carrol and Robert are a bull fight, with each man bringing out painful memories to taunt each other. As more about their shared past is revealed, the two morph from downtrodden friends to brokenhearted men with vengeful streaks. Wounded plays with the audience’s sympathies, never allowing us to rest easily in our conception of who was wronged and who inflicted the pain. Taggart and Jones are excellent scene partners, and they are mesmerizing to watch as they circle each other’s insecurities and lunge out at old wounds.

While some of the script felt like well-trodden territory, especially around homophobia in small towns, there were many beautifully crafted explorations of human connection and identity. In a particularly vulnerable moment, Robert shyly asks Carrol when he first knew that he was gay. Carroll responds with his signature, sharp laugh before explaining that he never had the coming out experience because he has always loved men. “Oh honey,” he says with a barbed slyness, “You might be gay. I’m a queer… And always have been.” At a time when we are seeing renewed attacks on queer people, and as stories like the kind told in Wounded are being suppressed, the show carries a poignant weight that is hard to shake even after leaving the theater.

WOUNDED – Written by Jiggs Burgess; Directed by Del Shores,

WITH: Kristen McCullough (Katie), Craig Taggart (Carrol), Shaw Jones (Robert)

Evan Frank (Set Design), Carter Ford (Light Design), Adam Matthew (Sound Design), Tori Moss (Production Stage Manager) and Miranda Shaffer (Assistant Stage Manager). Produced by SoHo Playhouse (Artistic Director Darren Lee Cole, Managing Director Britt Lafield) and Beard Collins Shores Productions (Emerson Collins, Louise H. Beard and Del Shores).

At SoHo Playhouse, 15 Vandam Street; (212) 691-1555, https://www.sohoplayhouse.com/. Through March 16. Running time: 2 hours 30 minutes.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Commissioned by Manhattan Theatre Club, Dakar 2000, by Rajiv Joseph, is a lie from beginning to end. The author lies to us for effect and the characters lie to each other and themselves, all leaving the audience on constantly shifting sand.

These lies we’re told are, “the guiding principle of most foreign policy.” Well thank you State Department, but this leaves the audience to hold everything at arm’s length, not sure what to trust, and not being involved nor care about the characters and their outcome. Without the personal charm of actor Abubakr Ali, this play would not be able to keep the audience’s attention.

The only honest thing on the stage was the set by Tim Mackabee which was built on a turntable and incorporated both indoor and outdoor settings. Its movement helped the story flow and added much-needed atmosphere to what could have been a stilted experience. All the dialogue takes place in confined spaces: an office, a rooftop, a bar, and a hotel room, and director May Adrales does a commendable job of creating movement (with the help of the set) within these confines.

It’s Y2K, on the eve of the year 2000, and many worldwide are standing by waiting for the world to end. US State Department employee Dina’s (Mia Barron) world has already come to an end with the bombing of the Tanzanian embassy in 1998 having lost several friends and the love of her life. She was supposed to be working at the embassy that day but was home with a hangover that saved her life. The investigation of the perpetrators has come to a standstill, “No longer a top priority,” and she is seeking revenge for the destruction of her world. Following the possible funder of the Tanzanian explosion, she is in Senegal. She feigns to get Peace Corps volunteer Boubs (Abubakr Ali) out of trouble for misappropriating government supplies to win his trust and in exchange for enlisting him in an espionage plot that involves, sedatives, disguises, breaking and entering, and fingerprinting an unconscious man to confirm identity.

These two characters never connect on any deep level but only feign to do so. The audience does the same.

—–

Dakar 2000, written by Rajiv Joseph and directed by May Adrales.

Starring Mia Barron and Abubakr Ali.

Technical: Tim Mackabee – Scenic Design; Emily Rebholz – Costume Design; Alan C. Edwards – Lighting Design; Bray Poor – Sound Design; Shawn Duan – Projection Design; Tommy Kurzman – Hair & Make-up Design.

Now playing at Manhattan Theatre Club, 131 W 55th Street, through March 23.

Tickets can be purchased HERE.

The run time of the show is 90 minutes, with no intermission.

title.rendered: ON THE EVOLUTIONARY FUNCTION OF SHAME

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Talk about Food For Thought.  This is one of those plays to which people will refer in the future and say, “How come it took so long for this story line to appear?”

D. A. Mindell states in his program bio that “His work aims to contribute to a canon for transgender artists to explore the breadth and depth of opportunity that cis artists have been able to pursue for centuries.”

He has achieved that goal with this production and then some.

Adam, a transgender man, is pregnant.  This fact is introduced as a fait accompli.  There is no fuss, only fact.  Mindell does not spend time in exposition and expects us to keep up.  Adam (Cody Sloan) and his partner Fox (The understudy Marx appeared in this role on the day I saw this show.  He was superb.)  are visiting the office of Adam’s sister Eve (Kayli Carter) who is a scientist as well as a gynecologist.  Within the first few minutes of this scene we know that Adam adores both his partner and his twin sister.  The fact that he is pregnant is taken in stride – we are the ones who must catch up.

Mindell leads us down the path of first pregnancy jitters as they co-mingle with family disturbances and medical research.  Everything matters, and problems are revealed with laser precision.  Eve’s research partner Margot (Imani Russell) is pulled into the mix as an autistic voice who cuts through the detritus Mindell reveals.  Everybody has an opinion, and no one holds back.

We learn that Eve and Margot have been focusing on genetic research (the name of the company is the Eden Project) that could change the lives of many an unborn as well as offer a myriad of tests that Adam might choose to have.

Adam does not choose.  You should pardon the expressions, but Adam is adamant.  See what I did there…?

As more information on Eve’s research is revealed, the thread of the beaded garment holding everyone and everything together begins to fall apart.  Mindell and director Jess McLeod team up to present us with a tale of enormous consequence told in straightforward language.  These characters are at once loving and sloppy, tender and clumsy, reassuring and suspicious.  This is elegant ensemble work that honors the author’s intention.

The tale of the contemporary Adam and Eve is bookended by the tale of the original couple.  Jordan Barbour as Adam 1 and Elizabeth Ramos as Eve 1 acquit themselves well as our ancestors.  The question for me is why were these characters included?  They add little or nothing to the contemporary story.  I am certain I am missing something here, but honestly, the contemporary play has more than enough food for thought.  Yeah, yeah I know “Shame” is in the title, but these two stories did not connect.

This contemporary tale is a smorgasbord of ideas that will accompany you for a long, long time.  It stands on its own with no apologies.

Get over to Second Stage Theatre and leave your pre-conceived notions at home.

ON THE EVOLUTIONARY FUNCTION OF SHAME

by D.A. Mindell, Directed by Jess McLeod,

Jordan Barbour, Kayli Carter, Elizabeth Ramos, Imani Russell, Cody Sloan and Ryan Jamaal Swain and on the day I saw this production Marx appeared as Fox.

Scenic Design by You-Shin Chen, Costume Design by Hahnji Jang 장한지, Lighting Design by Barbara Samuels and Keith Parham, Sound Design by Bailey Trierweiler

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

Coming home to oneself is the thread of two solo shows that make up Maiden Mother Crone now playing at The Flea.

The evening starts with Sugarcoated, created by and starring Jen Ponton, and ends with creator and performer Deborah Unger’s The Longer My Mother is Dead the More I Like Her.

Ponton’s Sugarcoated is her story of growing up with a judgmental father, mean school kids, and eventually, a boyfriend who would be both overly loving and extremely abusive. She takes us from her adorable precious seven-year-old self to her at thirty-six, leaving her husband and embracing herself as a woman in love with another woman. She had always had these emotional lures to other women but pushed them away. Her embracing of her lesbian self is the freedom and self-acceptance she had always been searching for to bring her closer to completeness.

Ponton reminds us that childhood can be horrific. Most of us were picked on, bullied, ostracized, and made fun of at some point in our growing-up years. This makes it easy to relate to this little girl who, because of her weight, was laughed at and cruelly treated.

Ponton’s set is a labyrinth of objects – notes hanging on string from the ceiling – that highlight the story being presented. Director Tessa Slovis moves Ponton effortlessly throughout The Flea’s space incorporating the audience as part of the story. Ponton wonderfully balances breaking the fourth wall while maintaining her power and stage presence. She is marvelously engaging with movement, words, and emotions as she takes us on her life journey. It is a story to remind us of all our journeys and our resilience … AND, to fall in love with Jen Ponton.

Unger’s The Longer My Mother is Dead the More I Like Her, directed by Dominick La Ruffa Jr., implies a mother we are all going to find horrible and abusive, but what unfolds is a mother who is doing her best, sometimes it is a mess with floundering and misguided attempts, but you never feel for one moment that this mother hates her child or doesn’t want the best for her.

The set is down to nothing with Unger creating the atmosphere of the story, taking on multiple roles of those that affected her life as a child and, as she grows up. Those that helped her understand the struggles of her mother and the love that was always there. There are some hilarious moments – as when she says she discovered the comfort of thumb sucking, “ Thumb sucking. My first addiction.” Yes, it is! An addiction for some, and for others, the pacifier became the vice. The first discovery of self-comfort.

Unger is out at a gathering when she gets the call that her mother is dying. It is that drive to her mother’s side that evokes the memories of a lifetime with her mom. Both the good and the bad. Unger grew up an Army brat which carries with it constant movement as her father is stationed in both Europe and America. That means the world is always changing, schools flash by as she is in constant movement, and new friends are briefly acquired and quickly slip through her fingers.

The staging felt at times unspecified and wandering. Unger is a skilled actress so the use of one prop again and again to specify when she was her mother was not needed. Her subtle changes in posture and voice said it all.

Both solo performances illustrate the business of life. Its highs and lows, its constant changes and adjustments. The restrictions of family, the weight of family, of all of us trying to fit in with one another, but mostly trying to fit in with ourselves.

Maiden Mother Crone written by and performed Jen Ponton and Deborah Unger, directed by Tessa Slovis and Dominique LaRuffa Jr.

Running Time: 2 hours and 15 minutes with intermission.

The Pete Theater at The Flea 20 Thomas St, New York, NY 10007 (Note that the concessions are cash or Venmo only.)

excerpt.rendered: Both solo performances illustrate the business of life. Its highs and lows, its constant changes and adjustments. The restrictions of family, the weight of family, of all of us trying to fit in with one another, but mostly trying to fit in with ourselves.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Safe House is the most hypnotic piece of 2025.

A red velvet curtain opens to a disheveled space of living. A landline phone rings.

The effortless craze and unhinged performance by Grace (Kate Gilmore), an unhoused, lonely young woman, carries this story, as the plot was more thematically shown over a presentation of her thoughts. A sensory enjambment. Grace transports herself through past memories and trauma as an act of coping. Healing; or unintentional reversal. Repetition. A spiral of alcoholism, failed relationships, the emotional toll of family, and of men. The stability in childhood, and its strain. We’re in a constant state of fog; she’s dreaming to escape her current state.

The performance itself is jarring, nonlinear, and surreal. It’s disgusting; it’s immersive.

Grace has made her current “home” on a handball court; but I can’t necessarily tell it’s a court. I know it’s outside, maybe in an alley, on pavement, somewhere junk is tossed. A fridge lays open on its side. Grace holds a child’s karaoke set–that plastic kind with the little corded mic. A white stuffed rabbit, Grace’s comfort. Garbage bins, garbage bags. There’s old lamps and 1980’s televisions stacked on each other. The same clip of Snow White meeting her Prince playing on repeat. Simultaneously, a half-dressed man is projected behind Grace, his voice fills us, her.

The performance could have ended 30 minutes earlier; it could have ran 30 minutes longer; I would have loved it just the same. It may have in fact been the seemingly quickest 90 minutes I have ever sat through.

The familial relationships she grew up with are unclear—an aunt that was seemingly once a figure she admired but “lost her head / The one who sat where you’re sat / The one who cracked because she dreamt.” 

“Voices that are real are patterned safe.”

Grace is pushed onto the stage atop a toilet, at the peak of a pile of junk. She puts on a crown.

She empties princess gowns from a trash bag over the stage. She slips a Cinderella dress over her hips.

These relics from childhood are safe.

Photo by Teddy Wolff

Grace crawls atop an armoire in underwear, climbs into a closet of trauma, returning to her past to escape life’s present state, and its background voices. The set changes from one scene of discarded items to another–two card tables and two folding chairs: one for Grace, one for her stuffed bunny. One moment I’m looking at a mess; the next I’m looking at stars dotting a night sky, the stage bare.

Photo by Teddy Wolff

This production–the lighting, the design, the set changes, the sound, literally all the creative elements of Safe House— is flawlessly executed. This experimental, stream of conscious performance executes the immersion of us into Grace’s head.

Every single creative element of this production is as deliciously jutting and unstable as Grace herself. Flashing and fogging, focusing and blearying. The sounds and music are real and haunting; it hurts: a German Shepherd aggressively barking, despite it being just a static projection, I can see it’s sharp teeth, it’s gums–

Men fighting, sirens, pounding on doors, they’re trying to get inside.

The video clips silently playing takes up the stage, becomes a part of the stage. Each movement, each of Enda Walsh‘s and Anna Mullarkey‘s lines and songs, each transformation is intention and faultless. Grace’s words appear on the screen, I hyper-focus on each one. Her stream of conscious songs, lyrics, are thrown up onto the stage. I’m here for it.

Written by Tony-Award Winner Enda Walsh; Composed by Anna Mullarkey.

CREATIVE TEAM: Jack Phelan (Videographer); KatieDavenport (Set & Costume Design), Adam Silverman (Lighting Design)  Helen Atkinson (Sound Design), Eoghan Carrick (Assistant Director), and Andrea Ainsworth (VoiceDirector).

KATE GILMORE as Grace.

Safe House is makes it U.S. premiere at St. Ann’s Warehouse,  45 Water St, Brooklyn, NY; it will run until March 2, 2025.

Tickets can be purchased here.

Safe House is co-produced by St. Ann’s Warehouse and Abbey Theatre, Ireland’s National Theatre.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

The title of this show, “Redwood”, is singular, not plural.  We normally refer to this wonder of the natural world in the plural.  “The Redwoods,” we say.  Here the title refers to one Redwood, and this tree deserves a Tony Award all her own.

Best Supporting Tree.

I am so not kidding.

The Tree is majestic (and best seen from the mezzanine) in the extreme.  She comes out of nowhere and disappears with grace and style.  It takes awhile for us to figure out how this is done, which does not dismiss the majesty of this magnificent structure.  The combination of scenic design by Jason Ardizone-West and video design by Hana S. Kim – is astonishing.

The human being in this production don’t fare as well.  Not because they are not trying – this is a gorgeous ensemble.  The actors lean on one another, literally and figuratively.  And three of them climb The Tree enough to make my palms sweat.

The story centers on Jesse (Idina Menzel) who is running from her wife, Mel (De’Adre Aziza) and the reality that their son Spencer (Zachary Noah Piser) died a year ago.  A considerable amount of time is given to the opening song, “Drive,” which, as the title suggests, is about Jesse driving away from her problems that she hopes will not follow her.

Spoiler alert: the problems do follow her.

Jesse ends up in the middle of a Redwood forest where she meets two canopy botanists, Finn (Michael Park) and Becca (Khaila Wilcoxon) who work IN the trees.  Way up in the trees.  Scientists of a  sort.  Within a few days Jesse convinces them to not only let her watch (this is private property so she is trespassing) but to climb herself.  Mind you the only training Jesse has is YouTube.  So we are dealing with a kind of fairy tale event.  This would be okay if it were clearly a fairy tale, but it is not.  We are yanked back into Jesse’s relationship with Mel and then flipped to Jesse’s experience with The Tree.  In other words – pretty much none of this is believable from the get go.

Perhaps if the script were stronger it would have made a difference.  The script, however is weak.  It lacks spark or intrigue.  Most of the text is exposition with very little action.  The music is about the same – tepid – with one bland song after another that is often accented only by Menzel’s considerable lung capacity.  These fine actors honor the text as well as the music (with a phenomenal hidden orchestra led by Music Director Julie McBride), but their efforts are not enough to raise the temperature in the room.

The only element of this production that is engaging, other than The Tree, is Jesse’s relationship with Mel.  This is due in considerable part to Aziza’s combination of talent, strength and empathy.  Hers is a powerful performance, so strong one wonders how and why Jesse would run away from Mel.  This relationship  could have been an anchor for the entire story, but here it is treated as a side dish.

De’Adre Aziza in REDWOOD; Photo Credit Matthew Murphy and Evan Zimmerman

With so much talent and effort put into a production, it is startling to see how far off the mark this production landed.

So yes, for me – a disappointment all the way around.

And not for nothing – people around me were tearing up as Jesse’s journey progressed.  The majority of of the audience was cheering and hooting after each number.  And of course there was a standing ovation at curtain call.

And that is why we love theatre.  For every audience member there is a unique also being seen.  Sometimes you agree with your fellow audience folks.  Sometimes not.

REDWOOD written and directed by Tina Landau, with music by Kate Diaz, and lyrics by Diaz and Landau, Conceived by Tina Landau and Idina Menzel, Additional Contributions by Idina Menzel.

WITH  De’Adre Aziza, Idina Menzel, Michael Park, Zachary Noah Piser, and Khaila Wilcox

Jason Ardizzone-West (Scenic Design), Hana S. Kim (Video Design), Toni-Leslie James (Costume Design), Scott Zielinski (Lighting Design), Jonathan Deans (Sound Design), Matthew Armentrout (Wig Design), Melecio Estrella, BANDALOOP (Vertical Movement/Vertical Choreography), Jennifer Weber (Dream Choreography), Tom Kitt (Music Supervision), and Haley Bennett (Associate Music Supervision), with Orchestrations and Arrangements by Kate Diaz and Music Direction by Julie McBride. excerpt.rendered:
The title of this show, “Redwood”, is singular, not plural.  We normally refer to this wonder of the natural world in the plural.  “The Redwoods,” we say.  Here the title refers to one Redwood, and this tree deserves a Tony Award all her own.

Best Supporting Tree.

I am so not kidding.

@graph.name: Tulis McCall
@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
by Tulis McCall

There are any number of reasons why you should get yourself over to “Liberation” by Bess Wohl and directed by Whitney White at Roundabout Theatre Company.  First of all, they take away your cell phone – and watching people give up their lifeline can be amusing.  Second, it is a story told backwards and forwards, because it is a universal tale.  Like every good piece of family lore it sweeps us out of our seats and into the past, all the while reminding us that we are in the present. It is time travel at its best.

And, of course there is the nudity that, by the time it arrives, is sweet and comforting.

Lizzie (Suzannah Flood) is our host because it is her story of her mother.  She reassures us that the phone deprivation thing won’t last too long.  She thanks us in advance.  And the story begins.

The time is 1970, and for those of us who are old enough we know exactly where we are.  Nixon is President.  Women are second class citizens (FYI women didn’t qualify for credit cards in their own name until 1973 – thank you Gerald Ford) and it doesn’t take long to realize that Ms. Wohl is telling us that things have not progressed as much as the early feminists hopes.

This IS the story of the early feminists.  The ones who came together because liberation was in the wind.  There were few leaders.  There were working women afraid to ask for more money or more responsibility out of fear of losing their jobs.  Hmmm… Gay women who were closeted.  Mothers who were angry that meetings were at dinner time.  One woman shows up thinking it is a knitting circle and decides to stick around.  One woman is praying that her green card will lead to being  a divorcee.  One woman is living with her retired husband who no longer disappears to go to the office.  He is underfoot and close to being murdered – by her.  Into this mix Wohl deposits Lizzie who is very much in the present while she makes a social call on this group.

Everyone of us has said “I wish I could talk to so-and-so about that thing that happened.”  “How did they manage keeping sane with children in the house?”  “How did the women stake out a place for themselves inside themselves?’

As the defenses begin to drop we hear these women discovering their voices in the safety of this circle.  This is NOT a therapy session.  This is an awakening with roots.  Forgive me for not singling out any one actor, because what Wohl and White have created is an ensemble tale executed with immaculate precision by this entire cast.  Wohl understands that feminism encompasses issues of race, sex, relationship, forgiveness, poverty, bullying and compromise – to name a few.  She understand it so well whe brings a man, Bill, into the story.  The strength and resilience of the feminists of the 1970 is astonishing and is due the grace and respect it deserves because we are ALL standing on their shoulders.

As one woman tells Lizzie:

It was a huge problem for us, the having you, the raising you, and the way you took so much for granted and let so much slide— not just the political progress but the community— the solidarity– I don’t know where that is now, maybe it’s there. Maybe it’s here. …

… But also, looking at you. All of you. And knowing that the things we said and did, the conversations we had, are still here? That they’re not over. Well, I guess that’s the solution. It’s the problem. And the solution.

These women are us.  I don’t care what your age or gender is.  This is a show to see NOW because we all need to be reminded of the fight at hand.  We need our strength to step into the circle.  This collection of women and the communal pot of riches they created is a good place to start.

Liberation by Bess Wohl, directed by Whitney White.

The cast of Liberation includes: Betsy Aidem as “Margie,” Audrey Corsa as “Dora,” Kayla Davion as “Joanne,” Susannah Flood as “Lizzie,” Kristolyn Lloyd as “Celeste,” Irene Sofia Lucio as “Isidora,” Charlie Thurston as “Bill,” and Adina Verson as “Susan.”

The creative team for Liberation includes David Zinn (Sets), Qween Jean (Costumes), Cha See (Lighting), and Palmer Hefferan (Sound).

Through March 30. Tickets for Liberation are currently available by calling 212.719.1300, or online at roundabouttheatre.org. For groups of 10 or more please call 212-719-9393 x 365 or emailgroupsales@roundabouttheatre.org.

By David Walters

Juliet: A Revenge Comedy is a hoot, a holler, and a romp of farcical proportions that will keep your head, your heart, and your funny bone active from beginning to end.

It’s amazing what, with only a bucket of creativity and nothing else, artists can come up with. A long oblong block sits on stage, and that’s it. What unfolds from there is a twisted tale encompassing the stories of Hamlet, Macbeth, The Tempest, Antony and Cleopatra, and of course Romeo and Juliet and imagining the locals of Verona, Egypt, a remote island in the Mediterranean, Scotland, and the state of “rotten” Denmark.

Characters in stories are alive only due to the imagination of the author. But once breath has been blown into their lungs, the games are afoot as to where they will go and what they will do.

Transported into this menagerie of places and stories by Shakespeare himself (Ryan Gladstone), we watch as Juliet (a charming Lili Beaudoin) falls in love, has sex, pretends to die, wakes up, and distraught over Romeo’s death, kills herself over and over and over again. This time loop wears on her though, and she breaks out of it with the realization that she is just a teenager and has only known this dead guy lying next to her for two days. She is able to break the force of the words on the page when she finds the book, The Collected Works of William Shakespeare, and goes on a quest rounding up a bevy of cohorts to find a better life and avoid the rapidity of her death by stepping into the worlds of Lady Macbeth, Ophelia, Cleopatra, and Miranda from The Tempest (all these and more played with precision and absolute fun by Carly Pokoradi). Toying with the absurdities in each story and using the power of words, they eventually find their way into a better life for themselves by taking the power of the pen from Shakespeare.

These players are playing at full tilt and the enjoyment of what they are doing spills out into the audience like a wave of fun getting us all wet in the process. No need to bring a towel, you’ll want to stay drenched long after you leave the theatre.

—–

Soho Playhouse’s yearly International Fringe Encore Series is in full swing again giving New Yorkers the gift of seeing some of the best shows from fringe festivals around the world without having to buy a plane ticket. They provide the opportunity for exceptionally talented artists, who have already won accolades at their particular festival, an extended run at an off-Broadway theater. This opportunity has led previous shows to further runs and Drama Desk recognition. I always look forward to this time of year as the selections do not fail to surprise and delight. Please take a moment to look over their schedule and do go see a show or two, or three, or four. There’s a reason they’ve been chosen for this festival. They’re all great.

JULIET: A REVENGE COMEDY is by Ryan Gladstone and Pippa Mackie and directed by Ryan Gladstone.

Actors: Ryan Gladstone, Lili Beaudoin, and Carly Pokoradi.

A Monster Theatre production running at Soho Playhouse until March 1, so be quick.

Tickets can be bought HERE.

By Victoria Lynne Dammer

The Diary of Anne Frank, presented at Algonquin Arts Theatre, is the hauntingly tragic story of a young girl’s life as a Jew hiding in Amsterdam during the Nazi invasion, told through her writings.

After coming to power, the Nazis forced Anne Frank, a teenage girl from Frankfurt, and her family to flee to Amsterdam. With the eventual occupation of the city, the family went into hiding along with several others in a tiny apartment above a warehouse. The 13-year-old wrote in several journals that revealed a teenage girl’s horrors, dismay, and everyday emotions as she was stuck in captivity.

Lisa Catalfamo gave a superb performance as Frank, a spunky, inquisitive, intelligent young girl who observed her changing body and was aware of her sexuality. Like many teenagers, Frank struggled with her animosity toward her mother, Edith (Lauren Friedman). However, the special bond with her father, Otto (John C. Short), shone through the performances by both Catalfamo and Short.

Jennifer Shrestha delivered a very engaging performance as Mrs. Petronella Van Daan. She portrayed the anguish of giving up her most precious material gift, her fur coat, to provide for the basic care of those hiding in the apartment with her. Sacrificing for others is sometimes hard, even when it makes the difference between eating and starving. The audience sensed the pain Van Daan experienced during Shrestha’s rendition.

Theatergoers could hear a selection of Frank’s diary entries throughout the show, bringing the story to life that is often only read about.

In reviews, the special effects and sound design are often discussed when the action on stage is not as good as in this performance. In this case, search sirens and the sound of trains during Frank’s many nightmares added to the overall sense of fear and despair for the Frank family and the others in hiding. It was a bleak existence that ended with all being sent on a train transport to Auschwitz-Birkenau in Poland.

It’s certainly fitting that her father, the only survivor of his family who spent two years in what the younger Frank described as The Secret Annex, shared her words with the world to continue her memory. Frank had dreams like other teenagers; she wanted to be a journalist or a writer, not a woman with a dull stay-at-home life.

Those dreams were cut short by Frank’s death a few months before the concentration camp where she was living, Bergen-Belsen, was liberated. One cannot help but wonder what this magnificent human may have done with her life had she lived.

Frank expressed she was grateful for the gift that God had given her “to express all that’s inside me.”

The tears and resounding applause in the theater confirmed the entire cast and crew expressed everything Frank wanted the world to know about her and her story.

The Diary of Anne Frank, a play by Frances Goodrich and Albert Hackett, was newly adapted by Wendy Kesselman and is now playing at the Algonquin Arts Theatre through February 22. Starring Lisa Catalfamo, John C. Short, Lauren Friedman, Kitana Samme Sultan, Dave Fretz, Jennifer Shrestha, Maxwell Devivo, Arielle Dymyd, Michael Gonzalez and Garrett John. Directed by Gina Lupi and produced by Julie Nagy.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Night Sings Its Songs, written by Nobel Prize Recipient Jon Olav Fosse, presents us with one disjointed, unhappy modern couple, in conflict for 70 minutes straight. The Young Woman (Susan Lynskey) claims her husband (Kyle Cameron) reads too much, sleeps too much, writes (poorly) too much, and is rejected by publishers too much. Although, this last one made me wonder if he even had an agent before cold-pitching to publishers (it’s recommended to go through a literary agent first)–but maybe the writer in me was just annoyed by this minor detail.

While The Young Man is jobless and spends his days on the couch, The Young Woman is on maternity leave; she goes for groceries and claims she goes out with girlfriends while she not-so-subtly hides an affair with another man, Baste (Ken King).

At first, The Young Woman references The Young Man moving in, and their appearance leads me to believe they are a middle-aged couple living together after the woman had their child. But, it turns out that they have been married for years, and they have known each other for many more years. I can’t determine how old this couple may be, and Fosse has only given them titles of “The Young Woman” and “The Young Man.”

Perhaps Fosse’s work in Norwegian was popular in a country and culture outside of America, or maybe, the Nobel Prize Recipient’s work was lost in translation, but this play is not something I would even consider calling entertainment. I felt uncomfortable, and sorry, for The Young Man, as he was constantly berated by his wife.

As soon as the performance started, I despised The Young Woman, and midway through, I realized that Cameron was given a very big job–one that is impossible to handle with this casting and writing. The Young Woman is written to carry the show, but her tone barely rose above a rehearsed, repetitive scolding. He simply didn’t have anything to work off of. The maddening, exasperating bashing of her husband made me want to leave where I was seated front and center. I felt like I was a teenager again, listening to my mother nitpick my every decision and unfailingly finding something negative on which to comment. It seemed Cameron was left with the bare minimum to work with: forgettable parents (Jenny Allen and Steven Rattazzi) who  briefly visited their grandson, a son who apparently did not even resemble him, and a rejection letter from a publisher. Any inkling of chemistry on-stage was absent, and I was left wondering to what level this was intentional–or if the chemistry of the actors had been an abandoned after thought.

The single aspect of this production that seemed to hold everything and everyone together was the set and lighting–it was clean, modern, and consistent. Although the few hours passing in a single night of activity seemed a bit unrealistic, the clock hanging on the living room wall grounded us in the life The Young Man spent in melancholy. The lack of set change rooted us in the routine of the couple’s life together, and how perhaps their only acknowledgment of each other’s presence occurred in that living room.

Susan Lynskey (The Young Woman), Kyle Cameron (The Young Man), Ken King (Baste), Jenny Allen (The Mother), Steven Rattazzi (The Father).

Presented by New light Theater Project.

CREATIVE & PRODUCTION TEAMS: Brian Dudkiewicz (Scenic Designer), Tom Driscoll (Assistant Stage Manager), Jennie Gorn (Sound Designer), Paul Hudson (Lighting Designer), Roger Lipson (Production Stage Manager), Caroline Mack (Producing Associate), Julia Squier (Costume Designer). Gama Valle (Casting Director).

Night Sings Its Songs will play until March 1, 2025 at Theatre Row, in Theatre One, at 410 W 42nd Street, New York.

Written by Jon Olav Fosse. Directed by Jerry Heyman. Translated by Sarah Cameron Sunde.

title.rendered: Program 9: Chain Theatre Winter One-Act Festival

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Program 9 of Chain Theatre’s Winter One-Act Festival has consistently played to sold-out audiences during this festival–and for good reason. Four plays–all one-acts of varying lengths–find similarity in how they’re rooted in our internal thoughts and ideas put on display, whether they’re forced or willingly released. Often, we see how characters in each performance hold their emotions from significant others, or how they even resist admitting to themselves.

Program 9 of this one-act festival opens with Escape (The Piña Colada Song), written by Erin Moughon. A couple is seated at a dining table; it’s uncomfortable, a bit awkward. At first I think they have been set up for a date or are waiting for other guests. But what unfolds is a break-up-turned-argument about who is breaking up with who. Their chemistry seems nonexistent, and I’m unsure whether this is intentional. One partner has a long history of breaking up with people—from one night stands to relationships that lasted months, “The Piña Colada Song” is motivation for the start and end of each. And, perhaps, they are even a serial item stealer…transfixed on exiting the relationship with an item that they seem to enjoy more than the person themselves. The audience is clearly displeased with this man’s personality; disgruntlement emerges from the audience as women behind me groans, knowing his now-ex-girlfriend has been caught in his trap.

Deary Diary, directed by Emily M. White, features Elizabeth McBryde, as Josie, and Kevin Cheng, as Pablo, of whom has also written this equally comical, charming, and spurring piece. I laughed through Pablo’s earnest dedication to his practice of selling sunscreen to strangers, in door-to-door style–dramatically rehearsing to a body of water.

We immediately know Josie is going through difficult emotions, that she’s holding something back. This production was perfectly cast; Josie’s dry state, her tone of grasping for anything to get her through the day. Seemingly reluctant to reach to find the light, we wonder if Pablo’s unassuming, bright, and chatty personality will make her smile. Despite their contrasting personalities, perhaps they have more in common than Josie assumes. Maybe, even, Pablo can give Josie hope as he opens up, himself. Dear Diary highlights how personalities can encourage us to unfold ourselves, how someone’s mental state can change from a simple interaction. The clash of Josie and Pablo’s tones amp up our laughter. I’m immersed in their characters’ developments as though I’m on another bench in Central Park, watching this connection be forged.

Photo Credit: Genda Lin

Last Train to Nevada, directed by Yibin Wang and written by Pascal Phoa, places us in an intense, life-altering decision between an Italian woman, Ida Boitano (Gwyneth Benitez-Graham), and her Japanese fiancé, Fred Korematsu (Pascal Phoa). It’s May 1942–a few months after the Pearl Harbor attacks–in Oakland, California, and the couple have planned to escape in order to marry, safely, in Nevada. The couple have rehearsed for the moment if Fred were to be questioned: he will need to lie about his identity, abandon the prospect of returning to his family, and inherently, abandon himself and culture. We are asked to question whether Ida truly loves him, or the idea of who Fred could be: the false, Caucasian version of himself. Will he remain true to his roots, or perhaps, will she abandon him before they even make that last train?

This piece, inspired by historical figures, including pioneer and civil reights leader Fred Korematsu, just touches the surface of what sacrificing for love looked like during WWII, as we are dropped into this emotional conversation between this young couple. I don’t feel the chemistry between these lovers, but there’s clear tension of race and stakes of being American.

Photo Credit: Pascal Phoa

The longest piece of the evening, Between the Wired Fence, written by Kevin T. Durfee, focuses on our aspirations and what we choose to leave behind as artists in exchange for stability. Sacrifices we make for ourselves, for our loved ones. Would our younger selves be disappointed in what we have become? 

“Sometimes I feel like I’m just passing through.”

This piece is split into scenes highlighting Sawyer’s lost self and her relationship with her partner–her partner who has clung to his wildly unique– strange and hilarious–and bold profession in the arts. He has maintained is artistry, while Sawyer has abandoned acting years ago. I appreciated the overarching theme of this performance that remind us the importance of weaving our passions and hobbies into our lives and prioritizing ourselves.

During a night alone at home, Sawyer is visited and cornered by her younger self. Will she make an effort to find her way back to the version of herself that both she and her husband miss? How can we even begin to find ourselves again?–when we are caught between the wired fence.

Sawyer’s husband is memorable, as he emerges in a later scene, wet and slippery in boxer briefs and metallic boots and a necktie to deliver a monologue. But, despite his strong presence, scenes of him and Sawyer apart and together felt disconnected and dotted, as though he served as comedical commercial entertainment but took time away from the overall focus.

 

Both virtual and in-person production of Program 9 are set for their third and final performance on February 22 at 5PM.

Tickets can be purchased here. This one-act festival runs through March 2, at The Chain Theatre, 312 W 36th St, New York. Program 9 is performed on the Mainstage 3rd floor.

ADDITIONAL CASTING AND DATES
ANNOUNCED FOR
FREE SHAKESPEARE IN THE PARK’S TWELFTH NIGHT
AT REVITALIZED DELACORTE THEATER

January 30, 2025 – The Public Theater (Artistic Director, Oskar Eustis; Executive Director, Patrick Willingham) announced additional casting today and the production dates ahead of this summer’s production of TWELFTH NIGHT, directed by The Public’s Associate Artistic Director/Resident Director Saheem Ali. Newly announced cast members include b, Bill Camp, Khris Davis, Junior Nyong’o (playing Sebastian to real-life sibling Lupita Nyong’o’s Viola), Daphne Rubin-Vega, and Moses Sumney. The production will reopen the historic, revitalized Delacorte Theater, with the first performance on Thursday, August 7. The production will officially open on Thursday, August 21 and run through Sunday, September 14.

Join us to revel in the midsummer madness as twins Sebastian and Viola survive shipwreck, revenge plots, and the trick doors of love. The Public’s Associate Artistic Director and Resident Director, Tony Award nominee Saheem Ali directs this joyful romp welcoming all of New York back to the magic of Central Park’s beloved theater. Be there when the stage lights turn on again at The Delacorte—a New York City classic—with this high-powered production of the Bard’s classic comedy.

I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: Transcription as Translation by The Orchestra Now

content.rendered:
By Ed Kliszus

A Night of Rediscovery and Sonic Brilliance

There are moments in music when the familiar is made fresh, and the well-trodden illuminate anew. Such was the case when The Orchestra Now took the stage at Carnegie Hall under the baton of Leon Botstein, a conductor whose boundless energy and intellectual curiosity have long fueled concert programs of unparalleled originality. In a program aptly titled Transcription as Translation, the Orchestra explored the art of re-imagining musical works for different forces, bringing forth a riveting evening of discovery, expression, and virtuosity. Each transcription is an extraordinary gateway to the composer’s intent, crafted from the inventive afflatus and imagination of assiduous cognoscenti. For example, tonight, the inimitable, world-renowned George Szell explains Smetana’s work to us by presenting it as an orchestra piece rather than in words.

On stage with Leon Botstein conducting The Orchestra Now in a program entitled Transcription as Translation at Carnegie Hall. Photo by Matt Dine

Explaining Music with Music

Enjoy this anecdote from a legend about an interaction between Robert Schumann and Franz Liszt to develop the example of George Szell’s articulation of musical meaning by transcribing a string quartet into a symphonic work.

One evening, Schumann played one of his piano compositions for Liszt. As the music unfolded, Liszt, the curious and analytical listener, interrupted at one point and asked, “What do you mean by that passage?” Rather than explaining in words, Schumann simply played the passage again. After a moment of reflection, Liszt listened intently and smiled and said, “Ah yes, now I understand.” This brief yet profound exchange highlights Schumann’s belief that music speaks for itself, resisting verbal explanation. Liszt—who often sought intellectual and programmatic meaning in music—found clarity through repeated hearing. It’s a moment capturing their mutual respect and the beautifully enigmatic nature of music.

Mily Balakirev: Suite on Pieces by Chopin

The concert opened with Mily Balakirev’s Suite on Pieces by Chopin, a work composed in 1910 as a loving homage to the Polish master. Balakirev, a key figure of The Mighty Five (Mily Balakirev, César Cui, Modest Mussorgsky, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov, and Alexander Borodin) infused Chopin’s works with a distinctly Russian orchestral voice.

Mily Balakirev (1836-1910) was a Russian composer, conductor, and teacher in 1909s. Public Domain

The Preamble (Etude) shimmered with delicate woodwind interplay, while the Mazurka pulsed with spirited lower brass and crisp articulations, expertly led by Jack Corcoran on bass. In the Intermezzo, the Orchestra channeled a nocturne-like dreaminess, with warm, expressive strings painting an atmosphere of wistful reflection, heightened by the sensitive phrasing of Sam Boundy on cello. The Finale (Scherzo) burst forth in a whirlwind of color, with bold brass gestures and deft dynamic contrasts ensuring an exhilarating conclusion. This was a Balakirev who both revered Chopin and made him his own.

Part of the string section. Leon Botstein conducts The Orchestra Now in a program entitled Transcription as Translation at Carnegie Hall. Photo by Matt Dine

Bedřich Smetana: From My Life – A Romantic Memoir in Sound

Smetana’s String Quartet No. 1 in E minor, From My Life, orchestrated in 1940 by George Szell, provided one of the most profoundly moving moments of the evening. Originally composed as an autobiographical tone poem, this work encapsulates Smetana’s personal joys, struggles, and ultimate acceptance of his deafness.

George Szell, conductor, of the Cleveland Orchestra (at Schiphol) 1957. Eric Koch for Anefo Public Domain

The first movement, Allegro vivo appassionato, opened with brooding tension, the strings imparting an intensity that foreshadowed impending misfortune. Samuel Frois, leading the first violins, shaped the impassioned lines with precision and depth. The second movement, Allegro moderato alla polka, was a buoyant contrast—a lively dance that transported the audience to Smetana’s youth. The third movement, Largo sostenuto, was deeply affecting, as the Orchestra soared in an expressive portrayal of love and loss, with Enoch Ng lending a beautifully resonant viola presence. The final movement, Vivace, transitioned from a joyous discovery of Bohemian national identity to an overwhelming sense of fate, brilliantly captured in the Orchestra’s dynamic surges and heartfelt phrasing.

Percussion Section. Leon Botstein conducts The Orchestra Now in a program entitled Transcription as Translation at Carnegie Hall. Photo by Matt Dine

Particularly striking was the Largo sostenuto, where Sam Boundy’s opening cello lines ushered in a haunting beauty supported by delicate string sonorities. The orchestral transcription, masterfully handled, retained the chamber-like intimacy while expanding its emotional breadth.

Beethoven’s Hammerklavier: Monumentality Reimagined

Few works in the piano repertoire rival Beethoven’s Piano Sonata No. 29 in B-flat Major, Op. 106—the famed Hammerklavier—in sheer ambition. Orchestrated in 1926 by Felix Weingartner, this rendition transformed Beethoven’s most expansive piano sonata into a symphonic powerhouse.

Felix Weingartner circa 1890. Public Domain

The first movement’s Allegro established an immediate presence, the orchestra rendering Beethoven’s dense motivic interplay with startling clarity. The Scherzo displayed broad brass and woodwind flourishes, a dance of bold rhythmic propulsion and witty exchanges. However, it was in the Adagio sostenuto that the full weight of Beethoven’s vision was realized. Here, the strings excelled, crafting a sound of deep introspection, every phrase laden with meaning. The finale’s Largo-Allegro risoluto, a fugue of incredible complexity, was executed with precision and bravura, the contrapuntal lines voiced with sonic clarity.

Botstein’s interpretation ensured that this was not simply a transcription but an homage to Beethoven’s evolving sonorities. The Orchestra delivered challenging trumpet and horn entrances with confidence, and the trombones and horns, led by Zachary Johnson and Jid-anan Neethai, respectively, provided a muscular yet refined underpinning.

The Virtues of Interpretation and Orchestral Balance

The Orchestra’s commitment to articulation and dynamics was exceptional throughout the evening. Whether in the softest pianissimo or the most forceful fortissimo, every section maintained balance and clarity for an exhilarating listening experience. The French horns, under the leadership of Ziming Zhu stood out, their tonal warmth anchoring key passages with noble resonance.

The brass and woodwinds shone in the Scherzo, while the lower strings and cellos provided the emotional underpinning in the evening’s more introspective moments. The Orchestra’s sensitivity to phrasing was particularly impressive, allowing every movement to breathe and unfold with natural momentum.

Winds and brass. Leon Botstein conducts The Orchestra Now in a program entitled Transcription as Translation at Carnegie Hall. Photo by Matt Dine

The Setting: Carnegie Hall’s Timeless Acoustics

With its storied history and legendary acoustics, Carnegie Hall was the ideal setting for this ambitious program. The warmth of the hall’s resonance allowed for the Orchestra’s full dynamic range to emerge, from the most delicate string passages to the roaring brass climaxes. Leon Botstein’s ability to sculpt sound within this magnificent space only enhanced the immersive experience.

A Maestro of Boundless Curiosity: Leon Botstein’s Vision

Leon Botstein’s programming exhibited an intellectual rigor and adventurous spirit that few conductors match. By curating works that explore the concept of transcription as Translation, he provided the audience with a rare opportunity to hear masterpieces in a new light. Presenting a program of such distinctive and rarely performed works takes courage. Still, under Botstein’s guidance, the evening never felt esoteric—instead, it celebrated musical evolution and reinterpretation.

As a training ground for the next generation of professional musicians, The Orchestra Now continues to prove its worth, offering concerts of insightful programming and exceptional artistry. Their performance at Carnegie Hall was yet another demonstration of their growing reputation as one of the most compelling ensembles of our time.

An Evening to Remember

Transcription as Translation was revelatory, from Balakirev’s poetic homage to Chopin to Smetana’s profoundly personal reflection on life, culminating in Beethoven’s symphonic transformation. The Orchestra Now, under the steadfast leadership of Leon Botstein, delivered an unforgettable concert filled with distinction, brilliance, and profound emotional depth.

The Isaac Stern Auditorium / Ronald O. Perelman Stage at Carnegie Hall. Leon Botstein conducts The Orchestra Now in a program entitled Transcription as Translation. Photo by Matt Dine

This was a night to cherish for classical music lovers and those eager to explore new sonic landscapes. As the final notes faded into Carnegie Hall’s luminous acoustics, the standing ovation was not just for the performance but for the power of music to transcend time to speak anew to every generation.

title.rendered: A Letter To Lyndon B. Johnson or God: Whoever Reads This First

content.rendered:
By David Walters

A Letter To Lyndon B. Johnson or God: Whoever Reads This First is a dynamite show with the precision of a drill team, the down-and-dirty depth of a coal mine, shared with lightness and finesse that at times could have been delivered like a slap-in-the-face, but instead touches softly like a feather on a slight breeze. This show is tight, very tight; barreling along as if you’re tumbling down a hill and the moments that seem like pauses, are just that you’ve been briefly thrown into the air on your downward trajectory and will soon crash to the ground and continue the mad tumbling. All though, a great ride.

It’s a joy to watch clown pair Xhloe and Natasha tell the story of growing up and what it means as their childhood gets left behind. Dressed in rag-a-muffin ground-in-dirt scout uniforms, their only set piece is a large tire that becomes a myriad of objects, barriers, and pathways, facilitating the dance and physicality of their storytelling. Presented in the round their, storytelling style brings the audience along for the ride creating intimacy and togetherness. What a great ride it is.

President Lyndon B. Johnson is a father figure to the boys as they experience friendship and grow through an idealized boyhood to become men. What the show ultimately presents is friendship and the great value of having such a thing in one’s life. It is both light and heavy, funny and dark, causing both laughter and tears. What more could one ask?

GO! There’s a reason this production has won so many awards around the world.

—–

Soho Playhouse’s yearly International Fringe Encore Series is in full swing again giving New Yorkers the gift of seeing some of the best shows from fringe festivals around the world without having to buy a plane ticket. They provide the opportunity for exceptionally talented artists, who have already won accolades at their particular festival, an extended run at an off-Broadway theater. This opportunity has led previous shows to further runs and Drama Desk recognition. I always look forward to this time of year as the selections do not fail to surprise and delight. Please take a moment to look over their schedule and go see a show or two, or three, or four. There’s a reason they’ve been chosen for this festival. They’re all great.

A Letter To Lyndon B. Johnson or God: Whoever Reads This First, written, directed, and performed by Xhloe Rice and Natasha Roland.

Exceptional lighting design, sound, and production management by Angelo Sagnelli.

Through February 22 at Soho Playhouse.  Tickets can be bought HERE.

excerpt.rendered:
It’s a joy to watch clown pair Xhloe and Natasha tell the story of growing up and what it means as their childhood gets left behind. It is both light and heavy, funny and dark, causing both laughter and tears. What more could one ask?

GO! There’s a reason this production has won so many awards around the world.

content.rendered:
by Tulis McCall

I recently went to Playwrights Horizons for a performance of “The Antiquities” a/k/a A Tour of the Permanent Collection in the Museum of Late Human Antiquities.

This is another case of, “Did I see the same play as the rest of the audience?”  I know I saw an elegant production that kept me hooked for all 90 minutes.  I also know that it left me feeling bleak.  Like Jordan Harrison‘s previous play, Marjorie Prime also at Playwrights Horizons in 2015, this is “a play of ideas and there is more discourse than dramatic action.”  The play takes us through several centuries of human development.  In each of these stops along the way, the humans consider themselves more or less on top of it.  Even in the face of death there is not the fear that we are all going to hell in a hand basket.

Harrison sprinkles hopelessness like the scent of poppies in the Wizard of Oz.  We are the observers and the observed.   I am reminded of the Hans Christian Anderson movie musical where Danny Kaye sang:

… here’s a tale of a simple fool, just glance at a page or two.
You laugh “Ha Ha” but you blush a bit
For you realize while you’re reading it
That it’s also reading you

There is not one moment where we are not aware that we are being fed some very serious ideas – and they are not the happy ones.  “Look alive.” we are instructed as the play begins, and nearly blush to realize what that means.

This is a stunning cast: Cindy Cheung,  Marchánt Davis, Layan Elwazani, Andrew Garman, Aria Shahghasemi, Kristen Sieh, Ryan Spahn, Julius Rinzel, and Amelia Workman.  I wish I could tell you exactly what parts they play, but for some reason they are only identified as Woman or Man with a number in the program  I am certain there is a reason for that, but it was lost on me.  The parts played by each number are identified in the script, but it still leaves the audience in the lurch.  Perhaps the larger message is that, because we are all human, both in the production and audience, that naming the actors is a waste of time and focus.  Jury still out on that.

Back to the cast – these fine actors weave themselves into the story as warp and woof.  Each actors plays several parts, and their work is so exquisite that you loose tract of the specific performers and see only the characters.  Astonishing work all around.  Bravo!

A note here about the set.  I have performed on the Playwrights stage, and I can tell you from experience that there is not a quarter of an inch of extra space ANYWHERE.  Paul Steinberg‘s set of wide swaths of what look like metal sheets is magic.  Pure and simple.  Enormous props by Matt Carlin appear and disappear like rabbits in a magicians hat.  How did they do that???I wanted to stop everything more than once and make  someone show me where that bar, or bed, or refrigerator came from.  If I had a hat I would take it off to this design team.

In addition, the costumes and wigs are perfection.  Each century is shown in precise detail.  We are free to immerse ourselves in the messages that Harrison is telegraphing to us.

We begin in the 1800’s and travel beyond today’s location in time.  When all is said and done we are reminded that we, like all the characters in this play, have deceived ourselves into thinking that we are the champions of our time.  We think we are the boss of us.  Technology is there to aid us maintain our positions.  We are wrong.

As the characters bid farewell and thanks, they tell us, in the gentlest way possible that we are not the champions of anything.  We are place holders.  We are a transitional species.

A sad ending that sticks to the bottom of your shoe no matter how far you roam.  As for me, I need a bit light at the end of the tunnel – even if it is a train coming in the other direction.  With “Antiquities” Harrison pulls the plug..  It is a wonder nobody keels over.

And yet – the play has been extended.  I say “Good for them.”  Theatre isn’t meant to makes us all feel better.  It is to take us feel, period.  Antiquities does that and then some.

The Antiquities by Jordan Harrison, Directed by David Cromer and Caitlin Sullivan

WITH: Cindy Cheung,  Marchánt Davis, Layan Elwazani, Andrew Garman, Aria Shahghasemi, Kristen Sieh, Ryan Spahn, Julius Rinzel, and Amelia Workman.

Paul Steinberg (Scenic Designer), Brenda Abbandandolo (Costume Designer), Tyler Micoleau (Lighting Designer), Christopher Darbassie (Sound Designer), Leah Loukas (Wig and Hair Designer), Sarah Lunnie (Dramaturg), and Jeremy Chernick (SFX Consultant).

At Playwrights Horizons through March 2.  Tickets HERE

THIS REVIEW was originally published in February 2022.  Because of an oversight on our part we were not able to review the current production at the Todd Haimes Theatre.  The cast and artistic staff remain the same, however, and we feel confident that this review still stands.

This is a remarkable show and we hope you will enjoy it as well as this review.  Tulis McCall, Editor

By Sarah Downs

If you were born in another country, would you be the same person?  What if you had immigrated, speaking your first language at home and your second abroad.  Would you be able to express your true self in both languages, or would you forever be a stranger in a strange land?  In her poignant comedy English, Sanaz Toossi dissects the intricate question of language and self expression with precise and poetic hand.

Language is an identity, a prop, a lens through which one experiences the world; it is a cloak, a weapon, a liability.  It is to be embraced — or is that conquered?  It is as much a barrier between people as a conduit to understanding.  Add to that the issue of accents, and the knife twists deeper.

In English the play, English the language represents ambition.  In Karaj, Iran, four adult students have gathered for their test prep class for the Test of English as a Foreign Language (TOEFL), chasing fluency in the language that will facilitate emigration to the west.  The TOEFL is no mere language exam; it is the passport to a new life.

Their teacher Marjan (a luminous Marjan Neshat) has one rule:  “English only.”  Marjan is a firm yet compassionate teacher.  She knows all too well how high the stakes are for these students, and is determined they should succeed.  Neshat portrays Marjan with uncanny naturalism and intelligence, unveiling layer after layer of nuance as the play proceeds.

Denied the opportunity to rely on their native Farsi, the students have to concentrate on new words, new thoughts.  Even as she champions English, however, Marjan, struggles not to disappear within it.  Roya (an elegant Pooya Mohseni), slightly older then the others, possesses an aloof dignity that hints at the intensity of her focus.  Her one goal is to to live with her grown son in Canada.  All she needs is better English.  Sweet Golna (Ava Lalezarzadeh), the youngest among them, excels at learning, while Omid (Hadi Tabbal) appears already to be fluent.  It is not clear why he is in this class.  Lalezarzadeh carries off Golna’s youth with both humor and innocence.  And yet Golna is deceptively wise.  Meanwhile there is prickly, complicated Elham (Tala Ashe).  Ashe gives a sensitive performance as a vulnerable woman whose competitive nature hinders her success rather than facilitating it.

English takes its time, gathering its energies without rushing.  Toossi’s brilliance lies in her capacity to illuminate the intangible without turning the classroom into, well, a classroom.  Director Knud Adams matches Toossi step by well-paced step, drawing concise, subtle performances from each of the actors.

Indeed, that restraint reflects the production’s economy of scale.  Quietly suffused with its own implicit drama, Marsha Ginsberg’s simple rotating set of a square classroom creates space as it also tracks time.  In its anonymity, the room is Anyplace in Anytown.  At a moment’s notice, however, the simple cube can be transformed by Reza Behjat’s deft lighting.  When bright daylight pours through the windows, the walls melt as the back-lit desk legs morph into an infinity of vertical lines, like a wheat field in the midday sun.  It is nothing short of stunning.

English is must-see theater.  An expertly written, thought-provoking examination of the relationship between language and identity (and so much more), beautifully acted and sensitively directed, this play will stay with you long after you have left the theater.

English, by Sanaz Toossi; directed by Knud Adams.  With Tala Ashe, Ava Lalezarzadeh, Pooya Mohseni, Marjan Neshat and Hadi Tabbal.  Scenic design by Marsha Ginsberg, costume design by Enver Chakartash, and lighting design by Reza Behjat, sound design by Sinan Refik Zafar.  Presented by Roundabout Theatre Company.  At the Todd Haimes Theatre through March  2.  Tickets HERE.

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
by Brittany Crowell

In Urinetown (the musical, not the place), it’s a privilege to pee.  Written by Mark Hollmann (music and lyrics) and Greg Kotis (book and lyrics) the show follows the rules of Hollman and Kotis’ previous improvisation work: forbidding the use of bad words and topical references.  What results is a quippy show that pokes fun at form and systems and can now, twenty-four years after it premiered on Broadway in 2001, be viewed as a sort of parable – an encouraging yet somehow, quite unbelievably realistic look at a group of people who stood up against the status quo, and all the ridiculousness that ensued.

Jordan Fisher as Bobby Strong; photo by Joan Marcus

“What if the law … is wrong?” Bobby Strong (played brilliantly by an infectious and inspiring Jordan Fisher) states to a series of gasps from the evil politicians who work with Caldwell B. Cladwell (Rainn Wilson).  Bobby is the second assistant at “Public Amenity #9,” one of the town’s lowest possible amenities, where folks can barely scrape together the cents to pay to urinate.  He’s grown tired of seeing the citizens of his town struggle to relieve themselves and many of them (including his father) have been carted away to the mysterious Urinetown (the place, not the musical).

Urinetown (the musical) then follows Bobby’s journey from zero to hero, citizen to revolutionary.  We are led by the narration of Officer Lockstock (played with crisp, hilarious timing by Greg Hildreth); the smarter-than-she-looks Little Sally (Pearl Scarlett Gold); as well as the head of Public Amenity #9, Ms Penelope Pennywise (played with great heft by understudy Tiffany Mann at this Sunday matinee performance); and the musical’s wonderful cast of characters who bring their own personalities to each role, teetering between politicians, schemers, and downtrodden revolutionaries-to-be. 

The set, by Clint Ramos, is wonderfully functional.  A series of port-a-potty doors in bright orange sit beneath the elevated orchestra and spread open in act two to reveal new, hidden environments; lighting by Justin Townsend brightens the doorways and highlights the action of the musical with colorful bars of light.  A large lit sign sits over the stage reading, “Urine Good Company,” the name of the endemically evil corporation that taxes citizens on their bowel movements.  Costumes by Sophia Choi highlight the disparity between our two worlds with uniformly grey suits in one coupled with colorful and dirty self-styled looks in the other.

And yet, despite the beautiful design and the stellar performances, I couldn’t help but feel that the piece was missing a sense of cohesion and didn’t quite hit the mark.  The cast, all wonderful in their own right, came to the table with different styles and energy levels, and that combined with the piece’s already difficult to perform self-awareness, didn’t allow the jokes or the meaning or the ridiculousness of it all to land.  Still, for fans of the show, or those like me who saw it in a high school performance over a decade ago, it’s fun to see it fully staged and realized on the great New York City Center’s Encore! stage again.

 

URINETOWN – music and lyrics by Mark Hollman; book and lyrics by Greg Kotis; Orchestrations by Bruce Coughlin

Directed by Teddy Bergman; Music direction by Mary-Mitchell Campbell; Choreography by Mayte Natalio

FEATURING: Greg Hildreth; Pearl Scarlett Gold; Keala Settle; Jordan Fisher; Stephanie Styles; Jeff Hiller; Josh Breckenridge; Kevin Cahoon; John Yi; Tiffany Mann; Jenni Barber; Daniel; Quadrino; Graham Rowat; Yemen Brown; Myralucretia Taylor; Christopher Fitzgerals; Rainn Wilson.

Scenic design by Clint Ramos; costumes by Sophia Choi; lighting by Justin Townsend; sound by Nevin Steinberg; hair, wig, and makeup by Tommy Kurzman and Suki Tsujimoto; music coordination by Kimberlee Wertz; production stage management by Cynthia Cahil.  Produced by Encores! At New York City Center: Mary-Mitchell Campbell, music director; Lear Debessonet, artistic director; Clint Ramos, producing creative director. Running through February 16: https://www.nycitycenter.org/pdps/2024-2025/urinetown/
