title.rendered: Immersive Mozart by the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

A Symphony of Sight, Sound, and Soul

In the grand spirit of concert-going, some evenings uplift the soul, enlighten the mind, and remind us why we gather in the temple of music. The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony, under the masterful direction of David Bernard, provided just such a night with their Immersive Mozart concert—an event of breathtaking intensity, cinematic scope, and sublime musicianship present at each Immersive Concert Program. More than just a performance, it was an intimate journey through Mozart’s inner world, unveiling his genius through raw emotion and dynamic storytelling.

Audience and musicians Interspersed for the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s “Immersive Mozart” concert experience at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in New York City. Courtesy Park Avenue Chamber Symphony.

The Vision Behind Immersive Mozart

Ever the affable host and insightful conductor, David Bernard greeted the audience with warmth and excitement. As he introduced the evening, he explained the immersive nature of this concert. This approach places audience members within the orchestra, allowing them to feel the visceral power of the music from within.

French Horns in the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s “Immersive Mozart” concert experience at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in New York City. Courtesy Park Avenue Chamber Symphony.

With a nod to Amadeus, the Oscar-winning film that reintroduced Mozart to contemporary audiences, Bernard framed the night’s program as a cinematic experience in sound. The film’s legendary opening motif—drawn from Mozart’s Symphony No. 25 in G minor, K. 183—set the stage for an evening of Sturm und Drang, masterful dialogue between soloists, and an orchestral palette painted with fiery passion.

Symphony No. 25 in G Minor: A Storm of Emotion

From the moment Bernard’s baton descended, the orchestra erupted into the electrifying opening of Mozart’s Symphony No. 25 in G minor, K. 183. The dramatic syncopations and urgent string tremolos created an atmosphere of immediate, unrelenting tension. G minor, a key Mozart employed sparingly, was reserved for his most storm-tossed expressions, making this symphony an early masterpiece of raw intensity.

Bassoons in the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s “Immersive Mozart” concert experience at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in New York City. Courtesy Park Avenue Chamber Symphony.

Seated among the musicians, the audience could feel the visceral pulse of the work. The horns’ ominous calls and the violins’ surging lines brought a story of turmoil and defiance to life. The second movement offered a lyrical reprieve, momentarily calming the tempest before the storm returned in full force. The finale’s furious energy built to a climax that left the audience breathless, proving once again that Mozart—despite his short life—could conjure a sound world that remains timeless.

Young Mozart holding a music book 1768. By Johann Eusebius Alphen, (Vienna 1742-1772). Elektromagikum, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Enchantment of Sinfonia Concertante

After the symphony’s turbulent grandeur, the stage was set for a moment of poignant beauty. Enter violinist Sean Lee and violist Katharina Kang Litton, who took center stage for Mozart’s Sinfonia Concertante in E-flat major, K. 364. From the first notes, their sound wove an intricate dialogue—violin soaring with a golden radiance, viola responding with depth and pathos.

Here’s a sample:

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Edward Kliszus (@openingnight.reviews)

Their playing was seamless, their phrasing deeply expressive. The second movement, an aching Andante, became a meditation on loss and longing, its melodies seemingly suspended in the air like whispered secrets. By the time the joyous finale burst forth, the audience was transported, basking in the sheer exuberance of Mozart’s effervescent spirit.

Violinists in the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s “Immersive Mozart” concert experience at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in New York City. Courtesy Park Avenue Chamber Symphony.

Symphony No. 40: A Farewell of Fire

The final work of the evening, Symphony No. 40 in G minor, K. 550, brought the concert to a towering conclusion. Its restless opening theme, instantly recognizable, carried the weight of existential struggle. The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony delivered a reading that was taut with urgency, filled with the chiaroscuro contrasts that define Mozart’s late works.

Conductor David Bernard with Soloists Sean Lee, Violin, and Katharina Kang Litton, Viola performing Mozart’s Sinfonia Concertante in E-flat major, K. 364 in the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s “Immersive Mozart” concert experience at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in New York City. Courtesy Park Avenue Chamber Symphony.

Bernard guided the orchestra with a masterful sense of pacing, allowing the music to breathe yet never losing momentum. The famed Andante unfolded like a nocturnal confession, while the Menuetto’s persistent rhythms built an inescapable tension. A furious, defiant, and exhilarating finale ensured that the audience left the hall awestruck.

Conductor David Barnard and soloists Sean Lee, Violin, and Katharina Kang Litton taking bows after performing Mozart’s Sinfonia Concertante in E-flat major, K. 364 in the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s “Immersive Mozart” concert experience at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in New York City. Photo by Edward Kliszus

The DiMenna Center: A Sanctuary for Sound

This spectacular concert found its home at The DiMenna Center for Classical Music, a venue revered for its pristine acoustics and intimate setting. Located in the heart of New York City, the center provides an ideal space for immersive performances, where every note is given room to resonate. The hall’s warm ambiance perfectly complemented the evening’s program, allowing Mozart’s music to envelop the audience in an embrace of pure sound.

David Bernard conducting the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s “Immersive Mozart” concert experience at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in New York City. Courtesy Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

A Tribute to Musical Excellence

At the heart of this unforgettable evening was the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony—a jewel in New York’s classical music scene. Under Bernard’s direction, the ensemble achieves a balance of technical precision and emotional depth, making each performance a revelation. Soloists Sean Lee and Katharina Kang Litton brought a radiant virtuosity that illuminated every phrase, proving that Mozart’s works, though centuries old, remain as vital as ever.

Looking left to the cello section in the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s “Immersive Mozart” concert experience at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in New York City. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Experience the Magic Yourself

Fear not for those who missed this astonishing night—the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony has an exciting season ahead. With a dedication to immersive experiences and a passion for storytelling through sound, they continue to push the boundaries of concert performance.

The double bass section in the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s “Immersive Mozart” concert experience at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in New York City. Courtesy Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

For more details and upcoming events, visit the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s official site here.

Final Thoughts: A Night to Remember

At its best, music transports us beyond time, beyond place—it becomes a direct line to the sublime. Immersive Mozart achieved precisely that, wrapping the audience in the colors, textures, and emotions of the 18th century while making it all feel vividly present. If Mozart’s music is a conversation across centuries, then Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony ensured that every word and note was heard with the clarity and passion it deserves.

Cellists in the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s “Immersive Mozart” concert experience at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in New York City. Courtesy Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

Immersive Mozart by the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

With Soloists Sean Lee, Violin, and Katharina Kang Litton, Viola

David Bernard, Music Director and Conductor
875 5th Ave, New York, NY 10065
(917) 740-7227

For tickets and information, go to  the 2024-25 Concert Season

Readers may also enjoy our reviews of The Magic of Immersion: Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s The Nutcracker, The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony presents Tales and Transformation, The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony presents Between Sea and Sky: Debussy’s Painters and Poets, and The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony performs Mahler’s Symphony No. 5.

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

Holst’s The Planets and Arnold’s Duo Piano Concerto

On a crisp February evening, the magnificent Cathedral of St. Ann & the Holy Trinity in Brooklyn became a portal to the cosmos. The Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra, conducted by Maestro Philip Nuzzo, took the audience on an immersive journey through the galaxies with Gustav Holst’s epic The Planets and Malcolm Arnold’s dazzling Concerto for Orchestra and Piano Duet.

The historic cathedral, with its vaulted ceilings and resonant acoustics, proved to be an ideal canvas for this sonic journey. The performance, which fused music, animation, and sheer virtuosity, left the audience breathless and awestruck.

The Virtuosity of Konstantin Soukhovetski and Slava Gryaznov

The first half of the evening showcased sheer pianistic brilliance. As internationally celebrated virtuosi, Konstantin Soukhovetski and Slava Gryaznov tackled Malcolm Arnold’s rarely performed electrifying Concerto for Orchestra and Piano Duet. Written in 1951, this playful yet intricate masterpiece balances dazzling technical wizardry with rich, expressive lyricism. Here’s a sample from a rehearsal with the BCO:

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra (@bkchamberorch)

Pianist Konstantin Soukhovetski, with The Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra Presents an Immersive Journey Through Sound and Space. Courtesy brooklynchamberorchestra.org

From the outset, Soukhovetski and Gryaznov brought remarkable chemistry to the stage. Their intertwining melodies danced across the keys with effervescent energy, seamlessly blending with the orchestra’s dynamic flourishes. The fiery final movement, marked by an exhilarating rumba rhythm, enraptured the audience. It ended with a flourish that seemed to ignite the very air within the cathedral.

Pianist Vyacheslav Gryaznov, with The Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra Presents an Immersive Journey Through Sound and Space. Courtesy brooklynchamberorchestra.org

The Planets: A Cinematic Soundscape of the Cosmos

With the opening bars of “Mars, the Bringer of War,” the audience was immersed in Gustav Holst’s awe-inspiring vision of the planets. The Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra, in a remarkable feat of musical storytelling, created a stellar sonic landscape, painting each celestial body with sound and using Holst’s evocative orchestration to transform the concert hall into a vast expanse of space.

A Galaxy of Sound: Orchestra and Choir in Perfect Harmony

Under Maestro Phil Nuzzo’s meticulous direction, the orchestra wielded a profound command over dynamics. The thunderous brass section, led by trumpeter Tiago Linck, delivered the ominous, militant force of Mars. At the same time, flutist Eva Ding and clarinetist Yu-Ting Cheng spun delicate celestial threads in Mercury, the Winged Messenger. The BCO achieved a climactic sound spectrum, bringing a full-bodied and immersive depth to each movement.

The ethereal Grace Chorale of Brooklyn, directed by Jason Asbury, lent a haunting mysticism to Neptune, the Mystic, fading into silence as though dissolving into the infinite void. The choir contributed an ethereal, spiritual quality to the orchestral timbre, seamlessly blending with the orchestra to elevate the experience, enveloping the audience in a transcendental moment.

Maestro Philip Nuzzi with the Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra. Courtesy @bkcvhamberorch on Instagram

A Visually Immersive Experience: The Cosmic Canvas

As if Holst’s music wasn’t already otherworldly enough, acclaimed visual designer Nico Lee projected mesmerizing animations onto the cathedral walls, transforming the space into a celestial wonderland. Known for her work with Kelly Clarkson and Sia, Lee’s artistic vision extended the immersive quality of the concert.

Vivid, swirling nebulas and planetary landscapes moved synchronously with the music, heightening the grandeur of each movement. From the fiery red of Mars to the soft, dreamlike blue of Neptune, the visuals deepened the concert’s transportive power.

The Cathedral of St. Ann & the Holy Trinity: A Majestic Concert Venue

Nestled in the heart of Brooklyn Heights, St. Ann & the Holy Trinity is more than just an architectural marvel; it is a sanctuary for the arts. Its soaring Gothic arches and reverberant acoustics made it the perfect venue for such an expansive program. Every note lingered in the air, amplifying the sheer magnitude of Holst’s orchestration and the crystalline beauty of Arnold’s concerto.

As the final celestial echoes of Neptune faded into infinity, the audience was left suspended in a state of rapture, hesitant to break the spell so masterfully woven. The Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra had done more than just perform; they had created an experience, a journey that resonated far beyond the final note.

The Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra performing in the St. Ann & the Holy Trinity Church. Courtesy @bkchamberorch on Instagram

A Stellar Cast of Artists

Special recognition must be given to the orchestra’s incredible musicians. Anna Majcherczyk (Concertmaster) delivered expressive, virtuosic solos while leading the strings with dramatic depth, while Georgia Bourderionnet(Principal Cello) provided a resonant, soul-stirring foundation between her enchanting solo work.

The brass and percussion, including Tim McCarthy (French Horn) and Hansol Choi (Timpani), added dramatic intensity and excitement, while harpistYeonhwa Chung provided moments of celestial delicacy. The musicians played with a precision and passion that illuminated the genius of Holst and Arnold alike.

The Leadership of Maestro Philip Nuzzo

Maestro Philip Nuzzo was at the helm of this extraordinary performance, whose expressive and precise direction guided the orchestra with clarity and passion. His deep understanding of the music allowed him to shape each movement with finesse, drawing out both the grandeur and subtlety inherent in Holst’s score. His seamless integration of the choir, orchestra, and visual storytelling resulted in a cohesive and emotionally stirring performance. The Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra flourished under his leadership, delivering an unforgettable night of stellar musicianship and artistic innovation.

A Night to Remember

The Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra continues to redefine the concert experience, blending masterful musicianship with innovation and immersive storytelling. This unforgettable performance of The Planets and Arnold’s Duo Piano Concerto was nothing short of revelatory, proving once again that music can transcend, inspire, and transport us beyond the stars.

For those who missed it, one can only hope this extraordinary program performed by world-class artists will be repeated. Until then, the echoes of this cosmic odyssey can resonate in the hearts of those fortunate enough to witness it.

Holst: The Planets. Courtesy @bkchamberorch on Instagram

Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra’s Immersive Journey Through Sound and Space

Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra

157 Montague St, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Phone: (718) 801-3811

For tickets and information, go to https://brooklynchamberorchestra.org/.

Readers may also enjoy BLIND INJUSTICE: A Riveting Tour de Force by MasterVoices, and The American Classical Orchestra (ACO), and Chorus performed J. S. Bach’s St. John Passion at Alice Tully Hall at Lincoln Center

title.rendered: American Classical Orchestra: J. S. Bach’s St. John Passion

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

A Night of Transcendence: The American Classical Orchestra Brings Bach’s Masterpiece to Life

The American Classical Orchestra (ACO) and Chorus performed J. S. Bach’s St. John Passion at Alice Tully Hall at Lincoln Center, New York City. Under the Direction of Conductor Thomas Crawford, the ensemble provided a sublime, inspirational performance with featured vocal soloists including Tenor Jacob Perry as the Evangelist, Bass Baritone Enrico Lagasca as Jesus, Bass Baritone Andrew Padgett as Pontius Pilate. The many arias of the work featured soloists, including Countertenor Reginald Mobley, Soprano Kristen Hahn, Tenor Alex Guerrero, Baritone Timothy McDevitt, Tenor Gene Stenger, Baritone Edward Vogel, and Soprano Elisse Albian.

The Origins of a Sacred Masterpiece

J. S. Bach’s St. John Passion, composed in 1724, was first performed at the St. Nicholas Church in Leipzig. It was the first Passion oratorio Bach composed after assuming his role as Thomaskantor in Leipzig, a position that defined his legacy.

Bach based the work on John 18 and 19, the Gospel’s account of Christ’s betrayal, trial, and crucifixion. Unlike his later St. Matthew Passion, which emphasizes Christ’s suffering, the St. John Passion highlights Christ’s divine presence, even amid tribulation. The music is exquisite, turbulent, and deeply symbolic, underscoring the tension between earthly anguish and heavenly redemption.

American Classical Orchestra- J. S. Bach’s St. John Passion at Alice Tully Hall._1209 Photo courtesy American Classical Orchestra- J. S. Bach’s St. John Passion at Alice Tully Hall.

A Libretto That Resonates Through Centuries

Bach seamlessly weaves biblical texts, chorales, and poetic arias to create an emotional and theological dialogue between the narrator, soloists, and chorus. The work features stunning recitatives and arias, showcasing individual expressions of grief, faith, and hope. The opening chorus, Herr, unser Herrscher, is a commanding invocation of Christ’s divine rule, setting a tone of grandeur and urgency.

Excitement and Anticipation

The inimitable Maestro Crawford, impresario and cicerone of the musical arts opened the program with insightful, inspirational comments about the St. John Passion. His clever repartee induced excitement and anticipation as he noted the work’s challenging marvelous arias, magnificent solos, and the chorus serving as the heart of the work. Crawford evoked chuckles as he asked the audience not to sing along to the familiar Bach chorales. He noted that the chorus will tell us that “all is well in the world.”

Historical Authenticity

Alice Tully Hall was filled with an audience basking in the authentic orchestral sounds provided by the ACO. Listeners luxuriated in the rich sonic intones of transverse flutes, 18th-century oboes and English horn, stringed instruments with gut strings played with restraint and precision, organ continuo, and harpsichord.

Segments of the work featuring vocal soloists with a simple accompaniment of bass, cello, winds, and continuo were exquisite, effortlessly transporting listeners to the provenance of J. S. Bach.

Jesus Christ in the Tomb supported by the Virgin and St John who are flanked by St Joseph of Arimathaea and Nicodemus holding the instruments of his Passion, H,1.29. by Marcantonio Raimondi, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Precision and Verve

Crawford conducted the ensemble with precision and vitality, invoking rich colors to the performance from the ensemble through his gestures and harpsichord passages. His attention to detail was evident as the concert unfolded. Blending the old with the new, microphones were ubiquitously placed to ensure perfect sonic balances.

Virtuosic Melismatic Passages

It was an evening of world-class artists. The chorus characterized their roles with enthusiasm and dynamism, articulating the afflatus of the Passion with precision, drama, and dignity. Bel canto, lyric tenor Jacob Perry sustained his effulgent, commanding role as the Evangelist through recitative and virtuosic melismatic passages with aplomb. Stentorian Bass Baritone Enrico Lagasco glowed in his vocal power and authority as Jesus. Bass Baritone Andrew Padgett delivered his role as Pontius Pilate with the expected commensurate assurance. Soprano Elisse Albian portrayed her roles with bright, expressive, lyrical precision and crystalline purity. Countertenor Reginald Mobley’s exquisite contributions were delivered with elegance.

A Cast of Thousands

All told, the bevy of soloists and chorus teamed with a superb orchestra was consistently excellent and provided an incredible, exciting, dramatic, and musical range of characters akin to the metaphorical aphorism, “a cast of thousands.” Remarkable indeed. The evening was a mesmerizing, ethereal panoply of sacred sublime artistry and the exquisite contrapuntal dialectics of Bach’s oeuvre. The Aria for Bass and Choir, #24: Eilt ihr angefochtnen Seelen (hurry you tempted souls) was spine-tingling as it raced along, featuring the full virtuosic power of Bass Baritone Andrew Padgett as Pilate, the chorus and orchestra, and their illumination of the blinding radiance of Bach’s genius.

The ACO Chorus: The Heart of the Passion

The ACO Chorus was vital in embodying the passion’s emotive power. With exemplary diction, phrasing, and dramatic expressiveness, the ensemble infused Bach’s sacred chorales and rhapsodic outbursts with unrelenting fervor. Whether delivering the raucous cries of the crowd or the devotional purity of the final chorale, their presence remained a guiding force throughout the evening.

A Performance to Remember

The American Classical Orchestra’s presentation of Bach’s St. John Passion at Alice Tully Hall was transcendent. The orchestra, chorus, and soloists imbued the evening with grandeur, emotional depth, and divine beauty. Maestro Thomas Crawford’s leadership ensured that every note resonated with historical reverence and artistic passion.

For those who attended, the performance was a reminder of why Bach’s sacred works endure—they speak to the soul, the intellect, and the heart. And in the hands of the ACO, the music soared, reaffirming their dedication to bringing Baroque masterworks to life.

American Classical Orchestra: J. S. Bach’s St. John Passion at Alice Tully Hall

Announcing!

“On Friday, March 28, 2025, the American Classical Orchestra will move to Carnegie Hall to give a landmark performance of the Mendelssohn Octet in Eb Major, Op. 20. This High Octane Octet work was written by Felix Mendelssohn when he was only 16-years old, and was dedicated to his dear friend, violinist Eduard Rietz, for his 23rd birthday. The unique work is scored for four violins, two violas, and two cellos, making it essentially a double string-quartet. This powerful work blurs the lines between chamber music and symphonic compositional techniques, and was actually re-scored for full string orchestra by the conductor Arturo Toscanini in 1947. The ACO brings a fresh look at this well-known masterpiece via historic playing techniques and the warmer sound of gut strings.”

Office: (212) 362-2727

For tickets and information, go to https://aconyc.org/.

title.rendered: Bodas de Blood: A Timeless Tragedy Brought to Life at Teatro Círculo

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

A Riveting Adaptation of Lorca’s Masterpiece

The walls of Teatro Círculo reverberate with the poetic anguish of Federico García Lorca’s Blood Wedding in a mesmerizing bilingual adaptation, Bodas de Blood. Brought to life by the masterful hands of Celeste Moratti, this production is a collaboration between First Maria Ensemble and Cambalache Theatre Company. The result? A spellbinding theatrical experience where raw emotion and artistic precision converge.

Here’s a quick preview:

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by First Maria Ensemble (@firstmariaensemble)

A Symphony of Passion and Tragedy

Lorca’s Blood Wedding is a tale woven from the very fabric of human suffering—love, fate, and the relentless grip of tradition. Moratti’s adaptation intensifies these themes, shifting seamlessly between English and Spanish, mirroring the cultural duality intrinsic to Lorca’s Spain. This linguistic interplay adds another layer of tension, enriching the tragic inevitability of the story.

Federico García Lorca at the piano. Granada. 1919. Colección Fundación Federico García Lorca

From the moment the Madre (played with heartrending intensity by Eric Alexander) first mourns the violence that has stolen her husband and son, the play grips its audience in an unrelenting embrace. The script’s poetic cadence finds its ideal home in this cast as they pour their souls into each verse, whispered plea, and agonizing cry.

The Power of the Ensemble

With an international cast representing seven countries, Bodas de Blood breathes with authenticity and universal resonance. Michał Walentynowicz’s Novio exudes youthful hope, countered by the haunting presence of Ryan Schaefer’s Leonardo, a man possessed by forbidden love. Their doomed rivalry plays out with the inevitability of Greek tragedy.

A scene from Bodas de Blood featuring Michal Walentynowicz (Groom), Ana Ordoñez (Death), Ryan Schaefer (Leonardo), and Carmen Ezcurra (Bride). Photo by Jonathan Slaff

Embodying the Novia, Carmen Ezcurra commands the stage with an emotional depth that leaves the audience breathless. Her delicate yet fierce performance captures the agony of a woman torn between duty and an inescapable yearning.

As Leonardo’s Esposa, Stephanie Del Bino delivers a performance that is as painful as it is powerful. Her silent suffering portrays Lorca’s keen understanding of the human condition.

A scene from Bodas de Blood featuring Michal Walentynowicz (Groom), Eric Alexander (Mother) Ensemble. Photo by Jonathan Slaff

A Visionary Director at the Helm

Celeste Moratti’s direction transforms Bodas de Blood into a visceral theater experience. Every movement, every pause, every glance speaks volumes. The stage breathes under her direction, with shadows and light dancing like specters of fate. Having honed her craft at La MaMa and The Living Theatre, Moratti brings a bold, immersive approach that honors Lorca’s spirit while making it profoundly relevant to contemporary audiences.

A scene from Bodas de Blood featuring Carmen Ezcurra (Bride), Ryan Schaefer (Leonardo), and Francesco Santalucia (Composer, live performance-synth and electronics). Photo by Jonathan Slaff.er (Leonardo), Francesco Santalucia (Composer, live performance-synth and electronics). Photo by Jonathan Slaff.

The Relevance of Lorca’s Tragedy Today

Despite being written in 1932, Bodas de Blood resonates with today’s world. It explores themes of gender roles, honor, and the inescapable weight of cultural expectations. Lorca’s words feel eerily prescient in a world still grappling with the tension between individual desire and societal duty.

The tragic heart of the story—a woman forced to choose between love and obligation—mirrors countless contemporary struggles. It speaks to those silenced by tradition, those who battle against destinies seemingly written in stone. This production ensures that those echoes ring loud and clear.

A scene from Bodas de Blood featuring Stephanie Del Bino, Hraban Luyat, and Celeste Moratti (Woodcutters). Photo by Jonathan Slaff

The Fusion of Music and Movement

A production of this magnitude is more than just words. It is the heartbeat of the drums and percussion, the cry of the sonic intones curated through state-of-the-art synthesizers, and the whisper of footsteps against the floor. Francesco Santalucia and Papaceccio provide a live score that pulses like the very blood in the characters’ veins. The haunting and hypnotic music underscores the drama, binding the narrative with an emotional weight that lingers long after the final bow.

Sandro Isaack’s movement direction elevates this experience, creating a kinetic energy that flows through every scene. Whether through the ominous woodcutters or the ghostly presence of the Moon and Death, Isaack’s choreography ensures that every motion serves the narrative. Excellent lighting, sound, simple sets, and costumes supported and refined the production

A scene from Bodas de Blood featuring Ana Ordoñez (Death), and Carmen Ezcurra (Bride). Photo by Jonathan Slaff.

A Must-See Theatrical Experience

Some productions entertain, and some sear themselves into the soul. Bodas de Blood belongs to the latter category. It is more than a play—it’s an invocation, a lament, and celebration of Lorca’s timeless genius.

For those seeking a theater experience that is both intellectually and emotionally fulfilling, Bodas de Blood at Teatro Círculo is an unmissable event. It reminds us why we tell stories and return to the stage repeatedly: to confront the inescapable truths of our existence.

Leonardo: Ryan Schaefer

Director / Adaptation: Celeste Moratti

Stage Manager / Social Media: Gabby Ostuni
Production Assistant: Antonio Cocuzza
Set and Costume Design: Raffaella Toni

**Where to Experience **Bodas de Blood: A Timeless Tragedy Brought to Life at Teatro Círculo

The production runs through February 16 at Teatro Círculo, 64 East 4th Street in Manhattan’s East Village. Get your tickets now and prepare to be transported into Lorca’s world, where love and death dance their fated waltz.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

The title alone would make a person want to go to this show.  And the fact the very smart Joy Behar wrote it makes it even more enticing. I remember the stories in her one person show ‘Me, My Mouth & I” over 10 years ago.  Especially that one-liner of appreciation from Steve Allen.  Good writing lasts.

Behar opens this Readers Theatre event by telling us that she interviewed women who were divorced, separated or widowed and compiled their stories into a show.  Works for me.  Many are the shows that have been created using this method. “Vagina Monologues ” for one.

So imagine my surprise to be disappointed in this production.  The performers were rock stars (Joy Behar, Tovah Feldshuh, Susie Essman and Adrienne C. Moore).  The material was lukewarm.

With the exception of Tovah Feldshuh’s “Wigged Out” and to a lesser extent Behar’s “The Touch” the monologues were litanies of boorish and sometimes dangerous behavior with which these women put up.  Until they didn’t or until they gave up.  If these were stand-up routines each would have lasted a few minutes.  As it is, the writing wanders from pillar to post until we lose the thread.

Some of these characters put up with outrageous situations for years.  Decades.  One woman lived in the country without heat until her son turned 8 and needed medical care.  Another stayed for at least five years while they redecorated the house.  Another marriage “got worse and worse but it lasted 20 years”. These pieces may have been based on real situations, but are there not stories where women put on their Big Girl Panties and took charge?   And could we not have a little of both?  Women’s experience is like our vaginas – expansive.

I heard myself thinking, “Why am I listening to this?”

We are living in a time when a convicted felon and serial sexual offender is the President.  I don’t believe this is a time to listen to women verbally reason their way through their victim hood.

Respectfully, I submit that listening to these stories is not inspiring.  Rarely funny in a deep way.  That they are based on true stories I believe.   The undercurrent, however, is that marriage is a predicament in which straight women can be trapped. This is a story of survivors, not champions.  That feels a little milk toast to me.  The writing feels careful.

Myself?  I want more depth, adventure, wild moves, failure, resurrection and what Rosa Parks referred to as the oak tree that resulted from the “nut that stood its ground”.

I want more pure Behar.

My First Ex-Husband by Joy Behar. Directed by Randal Myler

WITH A ROTATING CAST

January 29-February 23: Joy Behar, Susie Essman, Tovah Feldshuh, Adrienne C. Moore

February 26-March 23: Judy Gold, Susan Lucci, Cathy Moriarty, Tonya Pinkins

March 26-April 20: Veanne Cox, Gina Gershon, Jackie Hoffman, Andrea Navedo

MMAC Theater at 248 West 60th Street.

@graph.name: Tulis McCall
@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

I don’t read the PR (Egad!) materials sent o me for most productions I see.  I had enough of people telling me what to think in the Catholic Church.  These days I go in unprepared and wait to see what happens.

So it came as a surprise to me that I had seen a production of Lia Romeo‘s STILL last year   And I repeat what I said at that time.

Ditch the first act.

The very little that is accomplished could be swept directly into the second act with no one the wiser.

The first act is two lovers reunited in Washington DC after a few decades.  Mark (Mark Moses) is a successful, and more important DIVORCED, lawyer living in Colorado.  Kids are grown and he is looking for a new chapter that may be siting right in front of of him.  Helen (Melissa Gilbert) is a successful author with no children and no romantic relationship anywhere.  The flame is rekindled and the game is afoot.  We see this coming from the opening moments.  There is nothing new or intriguing here.  There is quite a bit of cutesy that feels appliquéd.  Neither of these characters is cutesy.

MARK MOSES and MELISSA GILBERT in STILL. Photo by Maria Baranova

Jump to scene two where there is a boatload of undigested history and present day politics (and I do mean present day) to make the entire cart tip over.  But it stays up, and that is because of some terrific dodge-ball writing by Romeo.  If these two were at a cocktail party and unknown to one another some blood might have been drawn.  But they are definitely known to one another.  The passion and caring is deep.  Instead of throwing a hissy fit or two and bolting out the door, these people go for the gusto.  They take no prisoners and at the same time they leave no bodies behind.

As audience members we can feel the ebb and flow of this decades old relationship being flung into the pool of the present, and dare I say threatening atmosphere, of what is surrounding us right now.  Romeo has updated her reference points (last spring’s production was mounted at a time when Biden was the presumed candidate and Musk had not taken his unlawful position as Hired Gun).  She shoots from the hip without favoritism.  Which is why the second scene  works so well.  Gilbert and Moses are fine partners who know how to thread the needle of relationships and politics.  They focus on the hope they can find and refuse to throw the baby out with the bath water.

We leave thinking as deeply about this couple, and our relationships unreal life, as they do about one another.  Most of us in the audience, myself included, have let go of friendships because of recent politics.  This show dares us to look beyond the boundaries we have created.

It just takes awhile to get there.

Still by Lia Romeo, directed by Adrienne Campbell-Holt

WITH Melissa Gilbert and Mark Moses

Scenic design by Alexander Woodward, costume design by Barbara Bell, lighting design by Reza Behat, and sound design by Hidenori Nakajo.

the 8-week return engagement is now playing at The Sheen Center for Thought & Culture’s Loreto Theater (18 Bleecker Street, NYC). Through March 23.  Tickets are available online at SheenCenter.org, by phone at 212-219-3132, or in-person at The Sheen Center box office Monday to Friday noon to 5PM and one hour before performances.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

The past and the present exist simultaneously at The Soho Playhouse’ presentation of Gil Scott-Heron’s Bluesology, a tribute to Gil Scott-Heron‘s work (who you may know from his iconic The Revolution Will Not Be Televised). The performance brings his wit, wisdom, power, and grit forward to today at a time when his words ring out as timeless. Where the struggles he talks and sings about haven’t dissipated, haven’t left us. Listening to his words and music that speak of the inequalities and difficulties of living, time seems to have become frozen and not moved at all.

Gil Scott-Heron (1949 – 2011) was a civil rights activist, spoken word artist, singer, musician, and author known throughout the world for his work, was gifted the title of the Godfather of Rap, and inducted posthumously into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a recipient of the Early Influence Award. This highlight show encompasses his creativity from 1970 to 2010.

The evening starts like a festive party with noise shakers passed out to the audience. This communal activity, shaking when showing appreciation for what is seen and heard, brings the audience together in a way that clapping doesn’t.  His gift of taking the daily news and turning it into social satire filled with truth, and attaching rhythms that were in themselves thought-provoking was part of his genius.

The evening then progresses like a roller-coaster bringing you up and down on a historical journey of lived truth that touches us where we live. It’s a touching evening that reminds us what we’ve come from and where we need to go.

Gil Scott-Heron’s Bluesology is a “theatrical reinterpretation” of Scott-Heron’s stories, memories, poems, and songs that emanated from the turbulent times in which he lived.

An opportunity not to be missed.

—–

Soho Playhouse‘s yearly International Fringe Encore Series is in full swing again giving New Yorkers the gift of seeing some of the best shows from fringe festivals around the world without having to buy a plane ticket. They provide the opportunity for exceptionally talented artists, who have already won accolades at their particular festival, an extended run at an off-Broadway theater. This opportunity has led previous shows to further runs and Drama Desk recognition. I always look forward to this time of year as the selections do not fail to surprise and delight and this year is no exception. Please take a moment to look over their schedule and go see a show or two, or three, or four.

Gil Scott-Heron’s Bluesology was directed by Phylliss Bailey Brooks.

The ensemble of dynamite performers includes: Victor Orlando, Gia Scott-Heron; Anthony ‘Da Boogie Man’ Rucker, Conney Williams; Lorenzo Frank; Yawo JandwaWatts, Art.Us Mansoir; The ORACLE, and Tuesday Conner.

The show will run for 75 minutes without intermission.

Now through February 23 at Soho Playhouse, 15 Vandam Street, NYC.

For tickets: https://ci.ovationtix.com/35583/production/1218258 – https://www.sohoplayhouse.com/

title.rendered: Blind Injustice: A Riveting Tour de Force by MasterVoices

content.rendered:
BLIND INJUSTICE: A Riveting Tour de Force by MasterVoices

A Landmark Opera with Urgent Themes

Blind Injustice debuted in New York, reverberating across a sold-out Rose Theater with a dramatic urgency rarely encountered in contemporary American opera. From its stirring opening intones to its heart-wrenching close, the performance was a triumph of musical and narrative synthesis, demonstrating the operatic form’s capacity to confront profound societal issues.

MasterVoices presents Blind Injustice, Jazz at Lincoln Center’s Frederick P. Rose Hall, Monday, February 3, 2025, 7:30pm. Photo Credit: Erin Baiano

A Dynamic Score with Emotional Depth

A Fusion of Musical Styles

Scott Davenport Richards‘ composition flows with a protean spirit, seamlessly merging jazz, gospel, funk, hip-hop, and Broadway musical idioms. These styles, rather than clashing, are expertly interwoven to evoke the emotional and psychological landscapes of the exonerees portrayed. The music pulsates with a raw energy reminiscent of Leonard Bernstein’s rhythmic propulsion, Count Basie’s bluesy swing, and Aaron Copland’s sweeping Americana. It is a score that transcends conventional operatic boundaries, capturing the Injustice, pain, and resilience embedded in the narratives of the wrongfully convicted.

The Orchestra and Chorus as Storytellers

The overture sets the tone with dissonant, fragmented motifs that mirror the fractured justice system, eventually blossoming into soaring, almost sacred choral lines. The 120-member MasterVoices Chorus, under Ted Sperling‘s expert direction, proved indispensable to the work’s power. Their presence ranged from visceral cries of Injustice to poignant reflections of hope and resilience. The virtuosic and finely attuned orchestra rendered the score’s intricate layers with precision, passion, and elegance

Marc Kudisch and the cast of BLIND INJUSTICE. MasterVoices presents Blind Injustice, Jazz at Lincoln Center’s Frederick P. Rose Hall, Monday, February 3, 2025, 7:30pm. Photo Credit: Erin Baiano

Musical Themes of Justice and Redemption

Richards achieves a haunting duality, simultaneously indicting a flawed justice system and celebrating the triumph of the human spirit. His use of leitmotifs reinforces the themes of imprisonment and liberation, threading the exonerees’ individual stories into a cohesive musical tapestry. Jazz-inflected brass flourishes punctuate moments of defiance, while Copland-esque strings underscore the vulnerability of those unjustly incarcerated. Gospel rhythms infuse the courtroom sequences, conveying both fervent belief and the oppressive weight of systemic failure.

Libretto: An Intimate, Relentless Truth

The Power of Words

David Cote‘s libretto is a marvel of economy and emotional precision, grounded in the raw, lived experiences of the exonerees. His words cut through the intellectual veneer of legal debates, directly engaging the heart. Each character’s arc is vividly etched, with moments of piercing poignancy—none more so than in the aria sung by Nancy Smith (Reilly Nelson), whose soprano voice rose like a phoenix, embodying both the despair of her wrongful conviction and the strength of her ultimate vindication.

Christian Pursell (Prosecutor) in MasterVoices presents Blind Injustice, Jazz at Lincoln Center’s Frederick P. Rose Hall, Monday, February 3, 2025, 7:30pm. Photo Credit Erin Baiano

An Ending That Lingers

The libretto refuses to offer easy answers. The opera closes with the searing question, “What makes a person?” — a phrase that reverberates long after the final note, challenging the audience to look beyond the spectacle and into the complexities of justice and humanity. Cote and director Robin Guarino consulted extensively with exonerees to ensure authenticity, incorporating verbatim quotes and firsthand testimonies into the text. The result is an opera that does not merely recount events but immerses the audience in the psychological and emotional toll of wrongful imprisonment.

Joshua Dennis (Defense Attorney) and Victoria Okafor (Alesha) in MasterVoices presents Blind Injustice, Jazz at Lincoln Center’s Frederick P. Rose Hall, Monday, February 3, 2025, 7:30pm. Photo credit: Erin Baiano

Performances that Soared

Standout Vocal Performances

The cast was uniformly stellar, with standouts including Christian Pursell as Prosecutor, who opened the show with commanding power and sheer virtuosity. Eric Shane Heatley, as Rickey Jackson, captured the vulnerability and quiet determination of a man unjustly imprisoned for 39 years. Victoria Okafor as Alesha delivered a luminous performance, her soprano effortlessly navigating Richards’ demanding melodic lines. Phillip Bullock as Derrick Wheatt brought a soulful gravitas, while Joshua Dennis, the Defense Attorney, balanced impassioned advocacy with a nuanced portrayal of a man battling a broken system. Tenor Orson Van Gay II as Laurese Glover’s soared with shimmering brilliance as he expressed and sustained a visceral emotional intensity in the stratosphere of his voice, earning immediate extended applause.

The “East Cleveland 3” from left: Orson Van Gay II (Laurese Glover), Miles Wilson-Toliver (Eugene Johnson), and Phillip Bullock (Derrick Wheatt) in MasterVoices presents Blind Injustice, Jazz at Lincoln Center’s Frederick P. Rose Hall, Monday, February 3, 2025, 7:30pm. Photo Credit: Erin Baiano

Beyond sheer volume, tonight’s soloists possess color and nuance—sometimes a dazzling squillo slicing through the orchestra like a golden sword, other times a floating pianissimo that defies gravity. They sustained notes with unwavering control, showcasing technical brilliance and deep emotional connections to the music. They left audiences breathless, moved, and forever changed by the magic of vocal artistry.

The Chorus as a Living Force

Sperling aptly describes the MasterVoices Chorus as both antagonist and ally. They elevated the production to a near-cosmic scale, embodying the collective weight of societal judgment. Their harmonies shifted seamlessly from a faceless mob condemning the accused to an ethereal force amplifying their cries for justice.

The cast of BLIND INJUSTICE. Photo by Erin Baiano. MasterVoices presents Blind Injustice, Jazz at Lincoln Center’s Frederick P. Rose Hall, Monday, February 3, 2025, 7:30pm. Photo credit: Erin Baiano

Ted Sperling: A Visionary at the Helm

Bridging Classical and Contemporary Traditions

Under the inspired leadership of Ted Sperling, Blind Injustice became not only a musical event but an emotional journey. Sperling, whose career bridges classical music and Broadway worlds, brought his signature artist and versatility to this production. His deep understanding of dramatic pacing and gift for drawing out subtle nuances and sweeping grandeur were fully displayed. Whether conducting operatic masterpieces or breathing new life into Broadway gems like The Light in the Piazza, Sperling uniquely unites diverse musical traditions. With Blind Injustice, he harnessed the power of the MasterVoices ensemble to create a performance that resonated far beyond the theater’s walls.

Thomas Capobianco (Clarence Elkins) and company in MasterVoices presents Blind Injustice, Jazz at Lincoln Center’s Frederick P. Rose Hall, Monday, February 3, 2025, 7:30pm. Photo credit: Erin Baiano

Production and Direction

Staging That Amplifies the Story

Robin Guarino’s stage direction was understated yet profoundly compelling, focusing the audience’s attention squarely on the characters’ humanity. Her dramaturgical choices amplified the libretto’s themes, creating a visual narrative as captivating as the music. Jason Flamos‘s lighting added a spectral quality, with shifting shadows evoking the prison walls and the oppressive machinery of justice. Attention to detail was apparent, from the smallest detail to the projection of subtitles above the stage.

A Minimalist Approach with Maximum Impact

The physical staging was simpler than a grand opera, but that was not a distraction. Costumes and staging were effective and compelling, with sets allowing the performers and the music to drive the storytelling. This choice underscored the opera’s central themes, stripping away artifice to expose the raw, undeniable truths at its core.

Members of The MasterVoices Chorus. Photo credit: Erin Baiano

A Resonant Message

An Opera That Demands Action

Blind Injustice transcends its medium. It is an artistic achievement and a call to action. The post-performance discussions with exonerees Nancy Smith, Laurese Glover, Clarence Elkins, and Rickey Jackson were vital to the opera’s message, grounding its art in lived experience. These conversations, as integral to the evening as the music itself, reinforced the opera’s urgent plea for reform.

Post performance discussion with Ted Sperling, David Cote, Scott Davenport Richards, Robin Guarino Eric Shane Heatley, Rickey Jackson, Reilly Nelson, Nancy Smith, Orson Van Gay II, Laurese Glover, Clarence Elkins, Thomas Capobianco in post-show conversation. Photo credit Erin Baiano

A Thought-Provoking Finale

The opera forces the audience to confront difficult questions about justice and redemption. As the final chorus swelled with the words “What makes a person?” the Rose Theater fell into a hushed stillness, an almost sacred silence filled with contemplation. The audience was not merely moved but transformed.

A Masterpiece of Justice and Art

In its New York premiere, Blind Injustice proved a landmark event, combining operatic grandeur with moral clarity. Richards, Cote, Guarino, Sperling, and the entire MasterVoices ensemble have achieved something extraordinary—a work that entertains and enlightens, urging us to confront the blind spots of our collective humanity. This is opera as it should be: urgent, unflinching, and transformative.

Orson Van Gay II (Laurese Glover) in MasterVoices presents Blind Injustice, Jazz at Lincoln Center’s Frederick P. Rose Hall, Monday, February 3, 2025, 7:30pm. Photo Credit: Erin Baiano

A standing ovation is not enough. This work deserves a sustained echo in our cultural consciousness. Bravo, MasterVoices.

BLIND INJUSTICE: A Riveting Tour de Force by MasterVoices

MasterVoices

57 W 57th St 3rd FL. STE 324, New York, NY 10019
(646) 202-9623

content.rendered:
By David Walters

“In the end of my dream, I was always running from a falling boulder, but if it’s with you, then maybe we could stop the falling boulder together.”

Hailing from Taipei, Taiwan, Shinehouse Theatre‘s presentation of The Whisper of the Waves now performing at Soho Playhouse, is a beautiful metaphorical offering of the ebb and flow of life, our aloneness and the connections we make to all that surround us (human, animal, plant, mineral). It’s as much a dance and movement piece as it is a play. With mesmerizing actor-created waves, ebbing and flowing through the merging of the ensemble it parts to reveal the disparities of everyday life (a man’s relationship with a plant, a taxi ride, a cat’s demise, and a failed infertility attempt). Whisper is a delight for the eyes and a salve for the soul. Theatrical poetry as an art form highlighting the individual and our society.

With a company of seven actors the play, like life, begins before you even enter. Frozen in a beautiful tableau, a chime sounds and the actors slowly come to life as earth, air, and water in a choreographed dance of life taking the audience and themselves on a journey of connection.

There’s that old aphorism, “We’re born alone, we live alone, we die alone,” though disheartening, it shines a light on the connections that we do make in this world and adds value and permanence to those connections as we stumble through our lives. If you’re alone, you can’t get on the ark.

“No matter who you are, alone or have company, when the flood comes, sitting, watching the tide surge, no one is lonely anymore.”

The Whisper of the Waves is an enchanting piece of art.

Soho Playhouse’s yearly International Fringe Encore Series is in full swing again giving New Yorkers the gift of seeing some of the best shows from fringe festivals around the world without having to buy a plane ticket. They provide the opportunity for exceptionally talented artists, who have already won accolades at their particular festival, an extended run at an off-Broadway theater. This opportunity has led previous shows to further runs and Drama Desk recognition. I always look forward to this time of year as the selections do not fail to surprise and delight. Please take a moment to look over their schedule and go see a show or two, or three, or four. There’s a reason they’ve been chosen for this festival.

—–

The Whisper of the Waves was written and directed by Po-Yuan Chung and choreographed by Emiko Agatsuma.

Performers: Emiko Agatsuma, Yung-Yuan Cheng, Chia-Yi Chen, Yi-Jan Wu, Yu-Chiao Chen, Wan-ting Chang, and Comei Liao.

Technical Director – Zeke Lee, Sound Design – Ming-Yi Chen, Costume Design – Yi-Chen Lee, Lighting Design – Ya-Yun Ko, Graphic Design – Luta Liu, and Sound Board – Jessamine Lin.

 

The Whisper of the Waves is running through February 2nd. Tickets can be purchased HERE.

Theatrical smoke is used during this production.

title.rendered: In Pour Taste: A Comedy Wine Tasting Experience

content.rendered:
By David Walters

At In Pour Taste, currently running at Soho Playhouse, there’s alcohol, music, alcohol, fun, laughs, and alcohol. Not necessarily in that order, but all bundled together for a fun-filled evening that can’t miss. Your ticket includes five wine tastings.

This is a show for you if you like wine, learning about wine, laughing about wine, or just plain laughing. It’s a great show to go to with friends as the drinks come with the price of the entertainment. But hurry as word is getting out and the shows are selling out.

The production was brought over from Australia to be part of the International Fringe Encore Series. Comedians Sweeney Preston and Ethan Cavanagh are joined onstage by New York wine expert Olivia White as they guide you through five wines specifically chosen for the show. You’ll learn about grapes, fermenting, tasting, and judging. No pressure though as you’ll also learn that there are really only two kinds of wine, wine you like and wine you don’t. It’s an improv show based on a series of questions to the audience about their viewpoints about wine and life. The answers are funny to start with, and as I’m sure you can imagine, get funnier as the evening progresses and the wine keeps flowing.

Preston and Cavanagh with their great sense of comic timing, charisma, and the personal chemistry between them, have been traveling the world performing at Fringe venues and have learned how to work a room. Of course, the wine doesn’t hurt. But it still takes a good deal of talent to take a bottle of wine and make a meal out of it.

By the end, you’ll be doing the Hot Potato and Cold Spaghetti. But don’t be afraid. You’ll smile while doing it.

—–

Soho Playhouse‘s yearly International Fringe Encore Series is in full swing again giving New Yorkers the gift of seeing some of the best shows from fringe festivals around the world without having to buy a plane ticket. They provide the opportunity for exceptionally talented artists, who have already won accolades at their particular festival, an extended run at an off-Broadway theater. This opportunity has led previous shows to further runs and Drama Desk recognition. I always look forward to this time of year as the selections do not fail to surprise and delight and this year is no exception. Please take a moment to look over their schedule and go see a show or two, or three, or four.

In Pour Taste is written and performed by Sweeney Preston and Ethan Cavanagh and will be running through February 9th. Tickets can be bought HERE.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

“How far can you run in five minutes?”

…”How long is five minutes?” you may ask, out of breath, just a minute into running for your life.

In Gaza, Mariam (Khawla Ibraheem) will have five minutes to get as far from her home as possible when a warning bomb sounds on roofs to signal a big bomb will soon hit.

Khawla Ibraheem has written this gripping monologue, playing Mariam, in the one-woman show A Knock on the Roof: an all-too-realistic account of a  young woman–who’s both a mother and daughter–navigating daily life in Gaza during war. Ibraheem’s monologue is effective; it’s physical, thought-provoking, emotional. So much so that as this piece concludes, I’m asking myself if this is memoir, put on in memory, in reflection.

Mariam trails her son, Nour, to the beach with his friends; we hear crashing waves and children’s laughter. Ibraheem’s parenting is chill but protective. We can sense that she too is still transitioning into the expectations of adulthood in Gaza. She obsesses over the “disgusting water” that is the sea her son, Nour, is definitely NOT supposed to play in and the cute innocence of Nour breaking his fasting with little snacks that turns into meals.

Mariam’s husband calls her daily; she’s clearly bitter that he is not there; he’s away at graduate school. She lives on the seventh floor with her mother and young son.

“Tomorrow will be clear and sunny…nothing will happen. Nothing will happen.”

But there’s the undertone of war, death, confinement. We sit at the edge of our seats waiting for the knock that titles this piece.

Mariam sets the stakes of living in Gaza, where nothing is yours. Where your freedom is anything but yours.

We watch her wait for electricity, for running water, for loved ones to return, for a way out, for the knock. She waits for a noise that will only prompt more waiting: waiting for the next war, waiting to see who survives, what survives.

The most memorable moments of this monologue is hyperfocused on Mariam acting “normal,” sitting in her chair (the only prop on stage) and suddenly running, running, her shadow racing down streets. The physicality that light and movement bring to the performance is pure power.

Photo Credit: Joan Marcus

Night after night, Mariam practices the five minute run with a sack of books, which soon is filled with belongings she couldn’t imagine leaving behind: skin care products that actually work for her skin, a dress, outfits, books for Nour, books for herself, toys, Nour’s clothing…five pairs of underwear. How many would you pack? she asks a woman in the audience.

Three.

Why three?

…

What would you take with you?

Ibraheem’s performance brings her poignant question to stage. It drops us into the “what if’s” of this urgency.

Someone from the audience speaks. “I’d just run.”

I appreciate how this isn’t a political play; it isn’t a Palestinian play; it isn’t a support-this-side-or-that-side play. It’s a play of thought and panic and connection to the audience. It was a piece of realism in literally any disaster, any war zone, any moment that immediately becomes life or death. It’s a reality check: the daily life of over 200 million people living in war zones.

I so love the stream of conscious, storytelling, Mariam’s thoughts diced and thrown at the audience, prompting us to silently ask ourselves what we would leave and what we’d take if we had to leave our homes in seconds.

What Mariam takes and forgets is unexpected. The few moments that are precisely life or death.

A Knock on the Roof , Written and Performed by Khawla Ibraheem.

Directed and developed by Oliver Butler.

A co-production with piece by piece productions
Presented in partnership with Under the Radar.  At New York Theatre Workshop through February 16.  Tickets HERE.

excerpt.rendered:
“How far can you run in five minutes?”
…”How long is five minutes?” you may ask, out of breath, just a minute into running for your life.
Khawla Ibraheem has written this gripping monologue, playing Mariam, in the one-woman show A Knock on the Roof: an all-too-realistic account of a young woman–who’s both a mother and daughter–navigating daily life in Gaza during war. Ibraheem’s monologue is effective; it’s physical, thought-provoking, emotional. So much so that as this piece concludes, I’m asking myself if this is memoir, put on in memory, in reflection.

title.rendered: The Day I Accidentally Went To War

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

The Day I Accidentally Went To War part of  Soho Playhouse’s Fringe Festival is an extraordinary life adventure told with side-grabbing shut the damn front door humor that will have you riveted to the stage. Comedian Bill Posley’s life experience is told with true-life images, movement, and his beautiful affable presence that will leave you feeling remarkable in many ways. This is a hell yes, must-see, for all! It is an inspiring performance of the resilience of us.

We are in a country that is unwinding and failing and yet we have tremendous potential of strength and the ability to reach out to one another and create love and acceptance. This is Posley’s unbelievable story of the complicated balance of life, the restrictions of parents, home, and the world of the military all holding the same contradictions, and yet Posley still being able to create and establish care and community.

Covering his life from a young child to an 18-year-old and beyond is this captivating, polarizing, one-man true story of durability, personal empowerment, and most importantly, the story of us, all of us on this planet. Bill Posley’s remarkable The Day I Accidentally Went To War is about those who go to fight the battles, the young men and women, so young that they are not allowed to order a beer in this country, but can carry a gun and, eventually, if they are lucky to survive and come home, they arrive in a place that does not recognize their struggles.

Posley is so attuned to the world and us because of his life’s struggles and experiences. He delivers them with his magnifying energy and sharpened skills as a comedian, writer, and storyteller.

He says the way to happiness is to accept one another. To recognize the struggles we all encounter and to admit to our neighbors, co-workers, friends, and strangers, when we are truly behaving like assholes and understand that YES we all will be an asshole at some point.

He grew up in a home with two loving but complicated, addictive parents. One struggling with drugs, the other gambling. He joined the Army National Guard to escape his home and pursue a college education. Instead, he received an education in strength and humanity. His time in Iraq was a hidden gem that led to an epiphany of love and acceptance.

The Day I Accidentally Went To War reminds us of those who serve(d) in the military. Their belief in this country and its people. And how most often they are made to be second-class citizens. Their mental difficulties having lived through the utter hell of war are dismissed and ignored.

Posley offers us one way to help veterans: go to veteranownedbusinesses.com and find a business near you that you can support. These are simple things to do in our complex climate.

In this hilarious and poignant performance, the audience is not an audience but recruits attending and experiencing the community and camaraderie of the military world. For the military to succeed, everyone must work together. Everyone must be there to have each other’s backs and protect and uphold one another, regardless of race, religion, or financial status.

The Day I Accidentally Went to War written and performed by Bill Posley, directed by Bente Engelstoft, producers Kristen Boulé and Suzee Dunn

Running Time: 90 Minutes no intermission Recommended for ages 14 and up.

Soho Playhouse 15 Vandam St. New York, NY 10013

Tickets for Fringe HERE

Bill Posley’s remarkable The Day I Accidentally Went To War is about those who go to fight the battles, the young men and women, so young that they are not allowed to order a beer in this country, but can carry a gun and, eventually, if they are lucky to survive and come home, they arrive in a place that does not recognize their struggles.Posley is so attuned to the world and us because of his life's struggles and experiences. He delivers them with his magnifying energy and sharpened skills as a comedian, writer, and storyteller.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

I spent time with Tennessee Williams and Marlon Brando last night. Together. In the same room.

In his expertly crafted play Kowalski, playwright Gregg Ostrin gives us the first meeting of these two theatrical icons prior to A Streetcar Named Desire‘s Broadway debut.

It’s nice to spend the evening watching a well-made play, with a spirited story, cleanly directed for tempo and clarity, played by wonderful actors, and dressed with a fully functional set that tells you where you are as soon as you sit down.

Robin Lord Taylor (as Tennessee Williams) and Brandon Flynn (as Marlon Brando) truthfully (and artfully) embody each of their characters in stance, speech, and mannerisms so that there is no question who is standing before you. Ostrin’s script gives them both the opportunity to take a wonderful ride together as they clash and admire each other, bouncing off their own egos as well as each other’s. Colin Hanlon‘s direction gives us no time to wander as we’re riveted to what these two are going to do or say next.

This play could also be called, “Abusive me and the women who love them,” but that’s more the subplot.

It’s the summer of 1947 in Provincetown Massachusetts where Tennessee has taken a house for the season with his director friend Margo (the exceptional Alison Cimmet) and boy toy Pancho (Sebastian Treviño). Tenessee has given Margo the unproduced script to Streetcar as he values her opinion. She says, “It’s brilliant.” He says thanks, but you can’t direct it, Elia Kazan is (cue priceless Alison Cimmet look). They eventually, kind of, patch this chasm in their relationship up and Margo goes off to a club with Pancho with Tennessee soon to follow. While he is in the other room Marlon comes into the house making himself at home in the cookie jar. He was sent by Kazan and had been expected three days prior, but he spent the bus money on food and hitchhiked his way there from NYC with a young actress friend Jo (Ellie Ricker, who is waiting for him at the bus station). After first thinking he’s a burglar and realizing it’s the long past overdue auditionee they get into the back and forth of, you’re too young for Stanley, and, I don’t want to do it anyway. These tennis volleys are of course the game.

Game, set, match. A wonderful evening in the theater about the theater.

—–

Kowalski was written by Gregg Ostrin and directed by Colin Hanlon.

The production stars Robin Lord Taylor as Tennessee Williams, Brandon Flynn as Marlon Brando,  Alison Cimmet, as Margo Jones, Ellie Ricker as Jo, and Sebastian Treviño as Pancho Rodriguez.

The creative team: costume design by Lisa Zinni, scenic design by David Gallo, lighting design by Jeff Croiter, sound design by Bill Toles, and movement specialist Nancy Renee Braun.

Now through February 16, 2025 at The Duke on 42nd Street at New 42 Studios (229 West 42nd Street).

Tickets can be purchased HERE.

I'm still enthralled by its gifts and process. I will endeavor to let you know whether I feel you should spend your time and money, acknowledging and rejoicing in artistic level and effort as a consideration. Thus, I may give a higher mark to the heart and soul of a college production than a Broadway show, holding each to a different standard. As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

title.rendered: American Symphony Orchestra: C. P. E. Bach at St. Barts

content.rendered:
By Ed Kliszus

A Night to Remember: C. P. E. Bach’s Legacy Revived

The magnificent St. Barts church on Park Avenue in Manhattan served as the perfect venue for an unforgettable evening of music. This historic landmark, renowned for its breathtaking architecture and superb acoustics, was alive with the sounds of C. P. E. Bach, masterfully brought to life by the American Symphony Orchestra. Maestro Leon Botstein, the orchestra’s Conductor and Director, opened the evening with a pre-concert talk that was both illuminating and engaging. His insights into the works of C. P. E. Bach painted a vivid picture of a composer whose brilliance transcended his time.

Leon Botstein. Photo by Matt Dine

Illuminating the Genius of C. P. E. Bach

Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach, the second son of Johann Sebastian Bach, carved his unique identity in the musical world. Unlike his father’s baroque complexities, C. P. E. Bach’s compositions incorporated bold harmonic language, rhythmic intensity, and poetic drama. Tonight’s program showcased two of his masterpieces: Heilig, H.775, and the U.S. premiere of Die Auferstehung und Himmelfahrt Jesu, H.777. These works reflect a daring blend of tradition and innovation, qualities that inspired even Mozart to conduct three performances of Heilig in 1788.

C. P. E. Bach’s contributions to the classical style—his adventurous use of sonorities, nuanced instrumental textures, and striking melodies—cement his place alongside Haydn and Mozart. As Botstein noted during his talk, these compositions remind us why his music is both timeless and transformative.

Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach (1733). Public Domain via Wikipedia Commons

The Venue: St. Barts on Park Avenue

St. Barts—a jewel of Manhattan—is celebrated for its historical significance and architectural grandeur. Its vast nave, adorned with intricate mosaics and stained glass, creates an intimate and grand environment. The church’s exceptional acoustics made it a favorite of Leopold Stokowski, a legendary conductor and organist who called St. Barts home for years. Those same acoustics elevated the performances to ethereal heights tonight, making every note resonate with clarity and warmth.

The Conducting Genius of Maestro Leon Botstein

Maestro Leon Botstein’s conducting was a masterclass in artistry and leadership. His ability to draw out the finest nuances of C. P. E. Bach’s compositions demonstrated an exceptional understanding of the music’s emotional depth and structural complexity. With precise, expressive gestures and a clear vision, Botstein guided the orchestra and choir to deliver a cohesive, emotive performance. His interpretation balanced historical authenticity with a fresh, contemporary energy, bringing new life to these 18th-century masterpieces. Botstein’s dedication to uncovering and revitalizing overlooked works enriches the classical music landscape and inspires audiences worldwide.

The magificent Nave at St. Barts. Photo by Edward Kliszus

The Choir and Soloists: Voices That Soared

The Bard Festival Chorale delivered a robust and moving performance. The chorale’s impeccable blend, diction, and emotional expression were fully displayed, filling the church’s nave with a celestial glow. Under the guidance of their skilled director, the Bard Festival Chorale brought C. P. E. Bach’s choral music to life with an energy that was both disciplined and passionate.

Leah Wool, Mezzo Soprano. Courtesy https:::www.facebook.com:LeahWoolMezzoSoprano

Their rendition of Heilig, H.775, was a highlight, showcasing their ability to balance reverence with exuberance. Four outstanding soloists—mezzo-soprano Leah Wool, soprano Mei Gui Zhang, tenor Terrence Chin-Loy, and baritone Troy Cook—complemented the choir.

Mei Gui Zhang, Soprano. Photo by by Dario Acosta.

Leah Wool’s rich, velvety tones added depth and emotion to Heilig. Mei Gui Zhang’s soprano soared effortlessly, her crystalline voice lending angelic beauty to her solos. Terrence Chin-Loy’s lyric tenor captivated with its warmth and resonance, while Troy Cook’s commanding baritone anchored the performance with gravitas. Together, they brought Die Auferstehung und Himmelfahrt Jesu to life, imbuing each phrase with expressive detail and profound sensitivity.

Terrence Chin-Loy, Tenor. Courtesy terrencechinloy.com

Troy Cook, Baritone. Courtesy troycookbaritone.com

The Orchestra: Virtuosity in Every Note

The American Symphony Orchestra, under Botstein’s baton, delivered a virtuosic and heartfelt performance. The orchestra’s ability to navigate C. P. E. Bach’s intricate textures and dramatic contrasts was remarkable. The woodwind section shone in its featured passages, with the flute and bassoon weaving mesmerizing counterpoints. The trumpets added brilliance and grandeur, their fanfares reverberating gloriously through the nave. Each instrumentalist contributed to an evening of musical excellence.

The Program: A Perfectly Curated Journey

The evening’s program began with Heilig, H.775, a choral work encapsulating C. P. E. Bach’s ability to balance reverence and exuberance. Following this, the audience enjoyed the U.S. premiere of Die Auferstehung und Himmelfahrt Jesu. This monumental oratorio, divided into two parts, narrates the resurrection and ascension of Christ with vivid storytelling and dramatic intensity. The juxtaposition of reflective arias and powerful choruses kept the audience enthralled from start to finish.

Leon Botstein with the ASO and Bard Festival Chorale at St. Barts. Photo by Edward Kliszus

A Tribute to History and Artistry

The audience erupted into a well-deserved standing ovation as the final notes echoed through St. Barts. The evening was a testament to C. P. E. Bach’s enduring legacy and the transformative power of music. The American Symphony Orchestra’s dedication to reviving overlooked masterpieces is a gift to music lovers and a tribute to the rich tapestry of classical music history.

Learn More and Stay Connected

For those inspired by tonight’s performance, we encourage you to explore more about the individuals and institutions involved:

content.rendered:
By Victoria Dammer

William Shakespeare’s play Cymbeline, also known as The Tragedy of Cymbeline, is often unheard of but significant in the Bard’s repertoire. Written in the early 1600s, modern critics classify it as a romance or comedy. Andrea Thome’s modern version combines many passions, including love, betrayal, jealousy, and other basic emotions.

Thome’s updated adaptation of the play transforms the original language into a format that modern theatergoers can enjoy. The National Asian American Theater Company (NAATCO) presented the all-femme, all-Asian American actors to the Lynn F. Angelson Theater stage. From the first act, the audience roared with laughter, thus proving Shakespeare’s imagination and understanding of human complexity moves forward through the centuries.

Fortunately for those who don’t know the story, the play began with a quick synopsis, but there is nothing like diving headfirst into a Shakespeare play. Cymbeline’s leading players are King (Amy Hill), his daughter Imogen (Jennifer Lim), and her husband Posthumus (KK Moggie), whom the king disapproves of. Cymbeline’s second wife (Maria-Christina Oliveras) and her dysfunctional son Cloton (Jeena Yi) are nefarious. The play is presented as a fairy tale, where intertwining plots and subplots keep you riveted by the action on stage.

The plot is uncomplicated. The King banishes Posthumus from Britain, and all bets are on whether Imogen will keep her virtue while he is gone. The Queen and Cloton try to interfere with the bloodline as Cloton attempts to woo Imogen. The Queen conspires to poison both Imogen and the King, securing her power as she manipulates her son.

There’s a gentle, sugary quality to Lim’s performance, a stark contrast to the treachery surrounding her. Ultimately, she gains the power to persevere in the Queen’s meddling and other players out to harm her.

Yi’s presentation of Cloten is unforgettable. Her body movements were so arresting that one cannot help but admire her tremendous acting skills and physicality. She caused uproarious laughter when she performed a song and invited two audience members to play instruments. She admonished the gentleman playing the tambourine and egged him on to play faster, much to the delight of all in attendance.

Olivera was a maddening tornado to reckon with as the Queen, a total powerhouse of a part, but not for long; she falls apart when Posthumus’s killing of her son ruins her plot. Moggie was exceptional, acting scorned but ultimately filled with remorse and love for the beloved Imogen.

The most significant factor in understanding Shakespeare is to attend any performance. Thome’s modern translation of Cymbeline is not to be missed.

NAATCO, in partnership with PLAY ON SHAKESPEARE, presents Cymbeline, written by William Shakespeare and translated by Andrea Thome.

Directed by Stephen Brown-Fried. Press by David Gersten and Associates.

WITH Purva Bedi, Annie Fang, Amy Hill, Anna Ishida, Narea Kang, Jennifer Lim, KK Moggie, Maria-Christina Oliveras, Julyana Soelistyo, Sarah Suzuki, and Jeena Yi.

Cymbeline is now playing at the Lynn F. Angelson Theater through February 15. Tickets can be purchase through this link.
