content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

If you already know Gary Gulman, and from the sound of  my fellow audience members last weekend 99% of them DID, you will be over the moon for this show.  If you ar not familiar you will still be charmed and entertained because that is the essence of Gulman.  Charming and entertaining.  This is not a bad thing.  Interspersed with the charm and entertainment is some damn funny and perceptive material.

This show is centered, one could almost say located, in Gulman’s home town of Peabody (pronounced PEA-buddy for you uninformed folks) Massachusetts.  Gulman was the third son way younger than the first two and spent time as a small child currying the favors of adults because he had no family interested enough in him to do more than offer critiques of his material.  It was a small town with his First Grade teacher living next door.  She had the extra key to Gulman’s house, let him call her by her first name away from school, and was the one who delivered the news that he was going to repeat the first grade at the insistence of his father who had moved out some years before, but still held sway over that family.

Storywise, things pretty much stop here.  That event stopped forward motion big time, and Gulman has spent more than a few decades pulling it all apart.  His ruminations are intriguing.  He had been the tallest kid in his original class and the second time around the situation took on grave proportions.  Kids thought he worked at the school for one thing.  And then there was the new First Grade teacher who picked the wings off flies in a former life, and in this life was content to torture Gulman over a misplaced library book.

No matter how far away this story wanders it always comes back to this period in his life.  Gulman rummages around this incident like a pig looking for truffles.  He mulls over the facts, turning the earth of the story over and over, picking out odd bits that take him down another path but not for long.  The one stone that is not turned is the fact that his father alone seemed to be in charge of the situation just on his say so alone.  His son was not mature enough said he. All these years later Gulman does not understand what that meant.  Perhaps it is too dark a path to investigate.

The second element toward which Gulman gravitates is books.  He shows us the first book he read by himself: “The Monster at the End of This Book” by Grover.  He was hooked by the very very very first page where Grover is pictured, saying “This is a very dull page.”  Gulman shows us the Sun Up book from First Grade that did nothing to save him from his incarceration.  In second grade he wrote “The Lonely Tree” which is, even today, his therapist’s go to.  So important to  him are books that the entire set is made up of five book cases of 10 shelves each, loaded with literature.  Except for one bookcase that is copped over and has spilled its largess all over the set.  Why?  Who knows.  

As this engaging choo choo train slides into the station we are brought back to Grover and Gulman who have both thought of themselves as the monster in the book, who both want us to enter but are afraid to ask.  Gulman’s vocabulary is way ahead of Grover. He twist and turns words like a magician about to pull a rabbit out of a hat.  He presents as uncertain, but he is uncertain like a fox.  Because in the end we discover ourselves back where we started with moments to spare.

Gulman is a chameleon.  While he feigns innocence, in the end he reminds us that all the while he has indeed been Grandiloquent (extravagant in language, style, or manner, especially in a way that is intended to impress) in plain sight.  A Magician indeed.

Grandiloquent – written and performed by Gary Gulman, Directed by Moritz von Stuelpnagel

Scenic Design Beowulf Boritt, Costume Design by Tilly Grimes, Lighting Design by Adam Honoré

At the Lucille Lortel Theatre through February 8.  TICKETS HERE

@graph.name: Tulis McCall
@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: College Fun A Very Late Post

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

College Fun, a witty send-up of buzzword culture, is a diverting one-act farce that immerses us in the frustrating world of obfuscation and apology that is modern “communication.”  Hamstrung as we are by the innumerable sensitivities of the professionally offended, we try to out-Woke each other — tiptoeing our way through conversation, in terminology that is both idiotic and ambiguous.  Good intentions and worthy values and ideas get lost in the cascade of extra verbiage.  The world of academia is particularly subject to every nuance of the minefield this creates.  (Don’t get me wrong; some of my best friends are Woke!)

As cancel culture has really begun to jump the shark, we find ourselves ever-the-more fearful that somebody, somewhere might not like what we say.  So we hedge our bets.  We preface what we say with caveats, and then preface those caveats with more caveats.  We outsource our thoughts to ‘thought leaders,’ our grievances to DEI counselors, our fears to safe spaces.  We unpack emotions and interrogate our feelings.  With all the self-doubt this creates, very little actually gets said, and almost nothing gets done.

All of this is played expertly for laughs in College Fun.  As the play opens, Professor Jones (a smoothly, slow burning DazMann Still) at a small college perched high in the clouds has been called on the carpet by the dean, Dr. Ram (a delightful Amy Frances Quint) for reasons unknown, and which remain largely unknown.  Nevertheless, Dr. Ram announces that Professor Jones must be canceled.  Let the games commence!

Dr. Ram is joined by Dr. Queeg (a powerfully energetic Jonathan Reed Wexler), a self-important, mercurial man who takes a brazen stance only to retreat a moment later, rather like a cat showing its tummy and immediately running away the moment you touch it.  Yet another dean, Dr. Pane (a wild-eyed Anuj Parikh), joins the fray.  Dr. Pane would definitely fail a stress test.  (One hopes the college keeps a defibrillator close at hand.)

Director Lynnea Benson balances the humor and frustration in playwright Ted Zurkowski’s clever writing.  Benson wisely reins in the energy periodically, giving us a moment to breathe and prepare for the next joust.  We can easily recognize ourselves in similarly perplexing and ultimately fruitless conversation, especially in the wake of Woke, and, you know Benson wouldn’t want us to be triggered or anything …

Each moment of recognition is limned by a frisson of danger, even as we laugh and sympathize in equal measure.  The actors up the ante with every pivot and parry in a dizzying, often self-referential sparring match.  That the conversation devolves into a form of “That’s for me to know and you to find out!” seems inevitable.  It is totally delicious, as one can hear the echo of its metaphorical twin:  “I know you are, but what am I.”   You wonder where it will end.

College Fun revels in a “Who’s On First’ of doublespeak, satirizing the truly irksome affectations that have permeated of modern culture –  which when you think about it is already a satire unto itself.  It is so satisfying to relax and just laugh at the absurdity.  As they say; if we don’t laugh, we’ll cry (especially now).  I giggled my way throughout this cleverly written ‘amuse bouche’ of a show.  I would love to see it in an evening of one-acts.  The play is timely and funny, and definitely should get some more air time.

College Fun, written by Ted Zurkowski, directed by Linnea Benson.  With Dazman Still, Amy Frances Quint, Jonathan Reed Wexler and Anuj Parikh.

Presented by the Frog & Peach Theatre Company, at Theater for the New City

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

Miss Julie 1925 New Year’s! is translator and director Robert Greer’s take on Strindberg’s masterpiece Miss Julie. At the time Miss Julie was first performed on March 14th,1889 it was groundbreaking, setting off a movement dubbed, “Naturalism.” The romance, the violence, the words of love and subsequent battling and belittling, and the struggle for evolutionary power are all packed into Strindberg’s 90-minute masterpiece. Greer’s translation stays close to the original (but tacks on a surprise ending), changing the location to the United States and the time to 1925. This new adaptation is set 100 years ago to this month when in 1925 confrontations between classes had taken on new levels of extremism. And here we are in 2025 with our own levels of class extremism.

This is a play about desperate unhappy people all reaching out to find the golden ring that will lift them out of their abysmal existence. They call forth, again and again, new ideas of themselves and how they wish their lives were, bouncing off of their hatred towards their reality of not only their rank in society but the expectations and chains that are part and parcel of their existence. All of this is done with words that fly and soar and repeat and repeat. To be aware of the repetition and find within it the subtleties that will keep the audience engaged is part of the difficulty of the marvelously flawed characters all asking for our attention and our worship. Difficult to accomplish. Sadly this production keeps the audience at arm’s length never allowing us in and so the characters and their struggles are flies on a wall for us to swat. There were several inappropriate laughs and smirks from the audience that only enhanced the lack of connection and truth between the actors on stage and the audience. On stage there was telling, displaying, and overachieving that eventually we the audience turned off and moved away from becoming observers and not partners to the production.

Theater for the New City has been a wonderful New York Theatrical space for new works since the 1970s. Marking the arrival of many of the theatrical world’s gods and goddesses. It has always been a space to try out, go for it, and see what happens, knowing that some pieces will hit and some will not. Ticket prices are still at such good rates it is the place for you as an audience member to try something out and see what resonates with you.

I am glad I went to Miss Julie 1925 New Year’s! It led me to rediscover Strindberg and his masterpiece. To sit and listen to the intricate words and stories of the characters and their life struggles is wonderful because hoping for more is a part of life and battling for it is what we humans do.

I urge you to go if you have the desire to increase your understanding of the history of theater and ask questions about class and individual importance to society. Although there are many flaws in this production, the essence of Strindberg’s work shines through emphasizing its intrinsic power.

Miss Julie 1925 New Year’s!  translator and director Robert Greer

With: Natalie Menna* (Julie) Mike Roche* (Jean) Holly O’Brien* (Christine)

Creative Team: Robert Greer (translator/director), Lighting Design – Alexander Bartenieff Costume Design – Billy Little Jose F. Ruiz – Stage Manager

Theater For The New City 155 First Avenue
(between 9th and 10th Streets)
New York, NY 10003

Tickets: HERE

Running Time: 90 minutes

title.rendered: David Dean Bottrell: A Teenage Wasteland at Pangea

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

In the intimate cabaret setting of Pangea in Manhattan’s East Village, David Dean Bottrell’s latest storytelling show, Teenage Wasteland, premiered on January 18, 2025. It’s a performance that feels less like theater and more like a long-lost friend confiding in you over a late-night drink. Bottrell’s talent as a raconteur has long been evident. Still, in this new show, his mastery over his craft reaches a fresh peak, blending humor, hilarious anecdotes, heartbreak, and raw honesty in a way that keeps audiences riveted from start to finish.

A Mirror and a Balm

The premise of Teenage Wasteland is as universal as it is specific. Bottrell focuses on his tumultuous teenage years growing up in the Bible Belt during the cultural upheaval of the 1970s. For anyone who has survived the awkwardness of adolescence—the heartbreaks, the insecurities, the desperate quest for identity—this show offers both a mirror and a balm. Bottrell’s storytelling is a time machine, transporting the audience to a period where every mistake feels catastrophic, and every small victory feels like winning the lottery. His gift lies in his ability to extract profound insights from the most mundane events, wrapping them in layers of humor, familiarity, and poignancy.

David Dean Bottrell. Courtesy daviddeanbottrell.com

A Portrait of Adolescence

Bottrell’s show is structured around five pivotal stories from his life between the ages of 13 and 15. Each tale is a microcosm of the teenage experience, blending comedy and tragedy. From grappling with a religiously devout family dynamic in a small-town factory setting to fumbling through social misadventures and first loves at school, Bottrell’s recollections are painfully relatable. His stories at the mall, in the choir, and in school theater productions are side-splitting!

Cheeky and Sincere

For instance, his confession about forging his parents’ signatures or skipping school. “If you never forged your parents’ signature, were you even really living?” he quips, eliciting knowing laughter from the crowd. But beyond the humor, Bottrell explores the deeper truths about adolescence—how it shapes our sense of self, for better or worse. His delivery, equal parts cheeky and sincere, makes it impossible not to laugh, cry, and nod along in recognition.

Every Emotional Moment Feels Authentic

Bottrell’s knack for balancing levity with gravity makes these stories stand out. A humorous anecdote about a failed romantic endeavor is juxtaposed with the sobering reality of growing up in a God-fearing family or reminiscing about old friends who have passed. Bottrell’s ability to weave these elements together ensures that every laugh is earned, and every emotional moment feels authentic. His stories aren’t just entertaining—they’re cathartic, transforming personal discomfort into communal healing.

Brutal Honesty and Boundless Empathy

What sets Bottrell apart as a storyteller is his frank honesty. He doesn’t sugarcoat the messiness of his teenage years or attempt to portray himself as a hero in these stories. Instead, he embraces his flaws, from his early days as a shy, art-loving “geek” who looked like “John Denver with the measles” to his later years as a rebellious, fun-loving, “dope-smoking, school-skipping bonehead.” His willingness to lay himself bare makes his stories resonate deeper.

As Therapeutic as Entertaining

Bottrell’s honesty is matched only by his empathy. While the show is deeply personal, it’s clear that he sees his experiences as part of a larger tapestry. Adolescence, after all, is a shared rite of passage, and Bottrell’s stories reflect the universal challenges of growing up. His empathy also extends to his audience, as he invites them to laugh at his missteps and their own. “The instant a group of people can laugh about something together,” he says, “you collectively release it. You forgive it.” This philosophy underpins the entire performance, making it as therapeutic as entertaining.

David Dean Bottrell at Pangea. Courtesy @daviddeanbottreal on Instagram. Click the photo for a Show Preview.

A Seasoned Performer at His Best

Bottrell’s experience as a performer is evident in every aspect of the show. Known for his roles in TV hits like Frasier, Modern Family, Mad Men, and Boston Legal, he brings the same charisma, stature, and sharp wit to the stage. But Teenage Wasteland is more than a showcase for his acting skills—a testament to his storytelling prowess and a kind heart.

Winner of the 2024 NYC Bistro Award and the Los Angeles Stage Scene Award for Outstanding Achievement in Storytelling, Bottrell has proven himself a favorite among critics and audiences alike. As Broadway World’s Nathan Johnson aptly put it, “Bottrell’s storytelling is a mesmerizing journey, unveiling subtleties and deep humor even in the darkest moments.” This sentiment holds for Teenage Wasteland, where Bottrell’s nuanced delivery ensures that even the most somber moments are laced with hope and humor.

The setting of Pangea, a cozy cabaret space with a great menu in Manhattan’s East Village, only enhances the intimacy of the performance. With its warm lighting and close-knit seating, the venue is the perfect backdrop for Bottrell’s heartfelt tales. The audience isn’t just watching a performance; they share an experience.

Bigger Than the Stage

While Teenage Wasteland is primarily a personal narrative, Bottrell’s decision to add two additional performances as fundraisers for the victims of the LA wildfires demonstrates his commitment to using art for a greater purpose. Having lived and worked in Los Angeles for 20 years, Bottrell profoundly connects to the community and knows several people who have lost everything to the fires.

“I’ve been donating to GoFundMe campaigns to the point where I’m tapped out,” he admits. “I just feel compelled to do a little more.” These performances, scheduled for January 21 and February 7, underscore the transformative power of storytelling—not just to entertain but to inspire action and foster solidarity.

The Future of Teenage Wasteland

Bottrell’s journey doesn’t end here. He’s already planning a sequel to explore his life from ages 16 to 18, promising more stories of heartbreak, hilarity, and growth. In the meantime, he has bookings lined up in Nantucket, Hyannis, and other locations this summer, ensuring that more audiences will experience the magic of Teenage Wasteland.

A Universal Truth

At its core, Teenage Wasteland is about resilience. “The basic formula of life is fall, get up, fall, get up,” Bottrell says. This sentiment resonates throughout the show as he turns painful, embarrassing memories into something beautiful and universal. By sharing his experiences with such honesty and humor, Bottrell reminds us that laughter can be a powerful tool for healing.

Whether you’re reliving your teenage years or simply looking for an evening of exceptional storytelling, Teenage Wasteland is a must-see. Bottrell’s knack for discovering humor and meaning in the chaos of adolescence is nothing short of extraordinary, making this show a triumph of both heart and artistry.

Tickets are still available for January 21 and February 7, but don’t wait too long—this is one journey you don’t want to miss.

Runtime is about 90 minutes.

David Dean Bottrell: A Teenage Wasteland at Pangea

Pangea

178 Second Avenue
New York, NY. 10003
Phone: (212) 995-0900

For tickets and information, go to https://www.pangeanyc.com/

title.rendered: Radio Downtown: Radical ’70s Artists Live on Air

content.rendered:
By Vahni Kurra

Radio Downtown: Radical ’70s Artists Live on Air is a satisfying blend of documentary storytelling and madcap character work that brings 1970s New York to life. Using archival recordings of Arts Forum, a WNYC program that featured interviews with avant-garde artists, the actors are tasked with recreating actual conversations, which are fed to them through ear pieces. The result is a wholly original production, presented at 59E59 Theaters, that manages to make a visual spectacle of radio.

While viewers may be more familiar with the zaniness of 1970s eccentrics like Allen Ginsberg and Abbie Hoffman, the production turns a spotlight on Benny Andrews’ smooth scree against the pigeon-holing of Black artists, Ed Sanders’ plan for exorcising and levitating the Pentagon, George Kuchar’s gruff eruptions of sexual profanity, Yvonne Ranier’s ponderous exploration of cinematic bodies, and so many more gems from the era. If you don’t know who these artists are, don’t worry. The lively debates and musings in the show provide all the color you need to understand what made each of them a force in the New York art scene.

Photos by Hunter Canning

The performances by Robert M. Johanson, Joshua David Robinson, Jennifer Morris, Maya Sharpe, and Colleen Werthmann were truly delightful. Each actor took on multiple roles, and all managed to capture the idiosyncrasies that made the larger-than-life characters really pop. The five-person cast moved around the stage with a great sense of physicality and comedic timing, perfectly complementing the offbeat conversation topics that ranged from blowing up New York monuments to weather-inspired erotica.

It was occasionally difficult for the show to maintain its momentum as the series of similarly staged scenes slipped into a lulling rhythm (much like a radio show). However, the play recovered from these plateaus with the electric energy of its actors. As the radio guests delved deeper into their conversations, the actors’ movements and choreography became more whimsical and unhinged, creating a kaleidoscope of ideas and visual metaphors.

The conversational snippets selected for the show were expertly curated. Some of the most poignant moments came from prescient conversations that reached through the decades and spoke directly to the concerns of a modern audience. In an exchange that felt like an omen, art curators Edward Fry and Ruth Bowman discussed a piece of computer-generated art with an interviewer named Stan. The curators were unimpressed with the computer’s clunky imitation of a Mondrian, and dismissed the idea that human creativity could be supplanted by it. Stan, however, insisted, “… this is not at all a science fiction possibility. It’s coming. It’s going to be here.” The poet Lorenzo Thomas’ description of computers creating a “vast store of trivialities” reminded me instantly of TikTok, Instagram, and the endless parade of content we now have access to.

Radio Downtown is a fun trip down the rabbit hole of ’70s New York art that reveals how much of this radical era is still with us today.

———

RADIO DOWNTOWN: RADICAL ’70S ARTISTS LIVE ON THE AIR – Written by Steve Cosson and Jocelyn Clarke; Conceived and Directed by Steve Cosson,

WITH: Robert M. Johanson, Jennifer Morris, Joshua David Robinson, Maya Sharpe, and Colleen Werthmann (Various Roles)

Scenic design by Andrew Boyce; costume design by Emily Rebholz; lighting design by Amith Chandrashaker; sound design by Ryan Gamblin; video design by Attilio Rigotti; movement director, Sean Donovan; production stage manager, Kate Wellhofer; assistant stage manager, Alexus Jade Coney. Produced by The Civilians. At 59E59 Theaters; 646-892-7999, 59e59.org. Through February 9. Running time: 1 hour 30 minutes.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Show Boat by Jerome Kern and Oscar Hammerstein II was first performed in 1927 and has stood the test of time with its music to still put a contemplative song in our hearts (Ol’ Man River), a spring in our step (Can’t Help Lovin’ Dat Man), and imbue a soul wrenching tear (Bill). It is considered one of the first stepping stones to the modern American musical utilizing song to further plot. Although the racial problems in the play, seen through our 21st century lens, are large speed bumps as the story progresses, there is a timeless and universal humanity in the love and care between people, the understanding of individual faults, and the pain that exists in daily life that keeps this show in the lexicon of American musicals.

Under the Radar Festival is presenting, through January 26, Target Margin Theater’s barebones revisionist production entitled Show/Boat: A River at NYU Skirball.

Despite this being first put on the boards in 1927, Show Boat covers the years 1887-1927 and its story and song transcend being a period piece as it holds a mirror to problems as a people that we still live with today. Show/Boat: A River strips away all that make it a period piece in order to try and make a point about our contemporary society. They didn’t go far enough.

If you plan on seeing it and don’t know the show intimately, please read a synopsis as it will help you understand the plot that at times gets lost in the minimalism of this production. There are a lot of confusing elements (staging, lighting, costumes, casting, set) that make this reinterpretation hard to follow at times and difficult to understand. You will come away with numerous questions about why the show was directed the way it was, no need to have the story be one of those questions.

Despite all the difficulties I’ve alluded to above, the story and songs do shine through and there is tremendous talent and effort put in by the actors which makes this production worth seeing, for the show Show Boat alone. But if you’re a complete traditionalist, this may not be the right one for you.

If you’ve ever seen an antique piece of furniture that is in the process of several layers of paint being sanded off of it, there are still traces of paint that remain, but the strength and beauty of the wood comes through in stark relief. That is my best analogy of this production. The cover has been taken off revealing strong bones, but it’s not yet finished.

—–

Show/Boat: A River is a play with music adapted from Show Boat (1927); Music by Jerome Kern; Book and Lyrics by Oscar Hammerstein II; Based on the Novel by Edna Ferber; Adapted & Directed by David Herskovits

Featuring an ensemble cast of ten actors playing multiple roles: Tẹmídayọ Amay,  Alvin Crawford, Caitlin Nasema Cassidy, Suzanne Darrell, Edwin Joseph, J Molière, Steven Rattazzi, Philip Themio Stoddard,  Rebbekah Vega-Romero and Stephanie Weeks.

Musical Director/Vocal Arranger Dionne McClain-Freeney; Musical Director/Orchestrator Dan Schlosberg; Costume Design Dina El-Aziz; Scenic Design Kaye Voyce; Lighting Design Cha See; Sound Design Megumi Katayama; Choreographer Caroline Fermin.
There is one ten-minute intermission.
Tickets can be bought HERE.

title.rendered: Sarah Anne Fernandez: Don’t Forget Me at The Green Room 42

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

Sarah Anne Fernandez took center stage at The Green Room 42 with her captivating new show, Don’t Forget Me. The show celebrated women’s legacy, resilience, and indomitable spirit throughout history tonight. Known for her commanding performances in musicals like Wicked, Fernandez’s latest endeavor demonstrated her remarkable ability to combine powerhouse vocals with heartfelt storytelling.

The 75-minute concert, directed by Rebecca Aparicio and music direction by Sheela Ramesh, was a deeply personal exploration of how women’s stories have been immortalized in musical theater. Fernandez challenged her audience to consider whether these portrayals reflect the true essence of women or how society chooses to remember them.

Opening with the premiere of an original song, Her Story, by Michael Mott, Fernandez immediately set the tone for a night dedicated to celebrating women’s achievements, struggles, and legacies. Accompanied by a skilled ensemble of musicians—Sara Overton (cello), Matt SanGiovanni (guitar), Brad Bosenbeck (violin), Nic Mrakovcic (bass), Jessie-Ray Leich (drums), and Sheela Ramesh (piano)—she delivered a masterful blend of Broadway classics and lesser-known gems.

Sarah Anne Fernandez on stage in her show Don’t Forget Me at The Green Room 42. Screen capture by Edward Kliszus

A Musical Journey Through History

Fernandez’s set list showcased her impressive vocal and emotional range as she brought iconic women to life through song. From Annie Oakley’s witty defiance in “You Can’t Get a Man with a Gun” (Annie Get Your Gun) to Maria’s empowering anthem, “I Have Confidence” (The Sound of Music), Fernandez honored each character’s strength and complexity through beautiful song.

She moved seamlessly from Gypsy Rose Lee’s playful charm in Let Me Entertain You (Gypsy) to Eva Perón’s poignant vulnerability in You Must Love Me (Evita). Her rendition of Heart of Stone (Six), a tribute to Jane Seymour’s enduring love and sacrifice, was a showstopper, showcasing Fernandez’s vocal prowess and emotional depth.

The performance also spotlighted lesser-known women, including sculptor Camille Claudel, whose tragic life was honored with Gold (Camille Claudel), and Tamara de Lempicka, celebrated in Woman Is (Lempicka). Fernandez infused these songs with reverence, ensuring their stories were told with dignity and grace.

Legacy and Connection

In one of the evening’s most powerful moments, Fernandez performed The Spark of Creation (Children of Eden), reframing Eve as a courageous figure whose curiosity shaped humanity’s destiny. Her ability to connect with the audience was evident as she spoke about each woman’s story, weaving a narrative of triumph, struggle, and legacy.

Fernandez’s portrayal of Marilyn Monroe in Never Met a Wolf (Smash) was sultry and poignant, reminding the audience of Monroe’s journey from foster homes to stardom. Her closing number, Keep Marching (Suffs), was a rousing anthem of resilience, leaving the audience inspired and uplifted.

A Performer’s Generosity

Fernandez’s warmth and authenticity shone throughout the show. She shared personal anecdotes, inviting the audience into her world. Her generosity extended beyond her performance, as she highlighted the contributions of her exceptional band and music arranger, Kim Scharnberg.

For Fernandez, Don’t Forget Me was more than a concert—it was a heartfelt, artistically profound portrayal in remembrance of the stories that shape us. Her commitment to connecting with her audience, soaring vocals, and compelling storytelling made the evening an unforgettable experience.

A Night to Remember

Sarah Anne Fernandez’s Don’t Forget Me was a triumphant celebration of women’s resilience, artistry, and legacy. With an eclectic mix of Broadway classics, original compositions, and deeply personal reflections, Fernandez reminded us of the power of music to heal, inspire, and connect.

Fernandez’s star burns brighter as she continues to forge her path in the theater world. Her ability to illuminate the stories of others while sharing her journey is a testament to her artistry and humanity. For those lucky enough to witness Don’t Forget Me, it was an evening that will not be forgotten.

Sarah Anne Fernandez: Don’t Forget Me at The Green Room 42

Written & Produced by Sarah Anne Fernandez
Directed by Rebecca Aparicio
Music Direction by Sheela Ramesh

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Vinny DePonto is a storyteller, a mentalist, and a pleasure to spend an evening with as he leads us through a show of memory extraction.

Mindplay, DePonto’s solo show comes to New York at Greenwich House Theater after sold-out crowds in Los Angeles and Washington DC. Mindplay is thought-provoking, playful, sentimental. It brings DePonto’s practice as a performer front and center–it shows his own human experience, while he helps us remember ours.

“Oh, how we fear the things we can’t control…your memories control you.”

Photo Credit: Jeff Lorch

DePonto’s show is ultimately a play with memory association: how his words stem a specific image or thought in our minds. My favorite exercise of memory association spurring stream of conscious thoughts–if only I had been able to connect more on a deeper level with those sitting around me, as those chosen to come on stage had.

He shows us his own mind: his memories of magic and memory, his childhood in upstate New York, significant time spent with his grandparents.

His fascination with Solomon Shereschevsky, a mnemonist from the early 1900’s,  inspired DePonto to begin his quest into gaining power over his mind. DePonto practiced (which he performs for us) memorizing pages and entire works of Shakespeare. He investigates how memories control what we fear, what we love, what we hide away. I would have loved for DePonto to dive into this research more, show us how we too can unearth specific memories, how to better hold onto them longer, or never forget them.

Moments when the audience participate together are the most evocative. When they feed off each other’s minds—literally. Taking seconds to stare into each other’s eyes before closing them and feeling exactly what the other feels. It garnered impressive reactions from the participants on stage; a feeling I wish to have connected with as an audience member. I’m sure the show was much more significant in their journey of recollection than mine.

One participant seemed a bit reluctant to buy into DePonto’s mentalis; perhaps he was even a bit in disbelief that DePonto was not just simply making general statements, leading participants to see a connection to whatever DePonto said. But when DePonto connected this participant to a much younger, international woman that he brought onto the stage, whatever guard or hesitations this man had completely fell. His face softened, and he genuinely smiled.

The woman, too, was equally if not more, in shock with how this other audience member had read her mind, with only emotional instruction from DePonto.

As another woman is selected, we listen along with this participant on stage, practicing sound association. Afterwards, the woman steps off the stage, pausing every few steps to look back to DePonto and smile in wonder, amazed with the specificity of DePonto’s mind reading.

Mindplay is a magic show, it’s a play, it’s an entryway. DePonto’s own memories that he withdraws from a literal wall of filing cabinets—memories that have been hidden away for decades are presented. He talks to the audience about how we too can pull those out. We’re reminded that the events we remember have become dramatic interpretations.

Photo Credit: Jeff Lorch

Over the 90-minute show, we’ve been dropped into a room we’re told that maybe we’ll remember forever, as a memory. Given the objects around the room, the backdrop, the props—we can use these as placeholders to remember the events, the people that move on and off the stage, the feeding off each other to draw from our own mind’s depths. DePonto reminds us how memories dictate our responses to events and emotions, but maybe there is a way we can at least control how we remember. While memories prompt the fear of the uncontrollable, healing can begin with memories: examining them with distance, from a different perspective.

 

Created and Performed by Vinny DePonto.

Written by Vinny DePonto and Josh Koenigsberg.

Directed by Andrew Neisler.

Performances begin December 15 for a limited engagement, running until April 20 at Greenwich House Theater, 27 Barrow St, New York, NY 10014.

Mindplay runs 90 minutes with no intermission.

Tickets can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

After seeing Audra McDonald as Rose in “Gypsy“, now at the Majestic Theatre, my companion mentioned that he didn’t see me take any notes.

“It’s too big for notes,” I said.

He concurred.

The element that is too big is, of course, Audra McDonald.

McDonald is the first in person Rose I have seen (other than the summer stock production at UCONN back in the day in which I played Tessie Tura), and I have to say I was astonished at what a beast of a show this is.  Two hours and 45 minutes of pure locomotive energy aimed at one place: The Spotlight.  And the billing and salary to match.  Do not get in Rose’s way if you value your life or your limbs.  She stops for no one.  Not her fiancé and certainly not her children, who we learn are interchangeable.

When we first meet Rose she is mid stride in bossing Uncle Jocko (Jacob Ming Trent), the host of a kiddie shoe in Seattle, around in order to better suit her daughter Baby June’s (Jade Smith as the younger at our performance and Jordan Tyson the older) voice and talent.  Neither of which amount to much more than annoying – but to Rose they are monumental.  While pushing her daughters June and, by asociation, Louise (Summer Rae Daney as the younger at our performance and Joy Woods as the older) along the track she stumbles upon Herbie (Danny Burstein) a shy candy salesman looking for someone to love and provide for.  While Rose has little interest in being provided for, other than legit bookings for her girls, she steps into Herbie’s life and brings him into hers.

Soon we are looking at a older teenage cast of June’s act (through a clever bit of staging) featuring Baby June, Louise and some talented young men who can dance their socks off.  They all climb and fall over and over again until the troupe colapses because they see the death of vaudeville writing on the walls.  Rose does not.

Danny Burstein, Joy Woods & Audra McDonald – Photo by Julieta Cervantes

Rose never takes off her blinders.  Instead she switches horses to focus on her daughter Louise, who will become the famous stripper Gypsy Rose Lee, noted more for what she didn’t reveal than what she did.  Success and fame have their price, however, as Rose loses her role in her daughter’s life and discovers herself an orphan with no one beside her.

As I said the center of this storm is McDonald.  She is the locomotive that pulls this show along.  She is so much the center that everything else, including the cast members pretty much pale in comparison.  Danny Burstein is a standout all around.  Herbie’s devotion to Rose is so deep that when it shatters you can feel your heart break.  Another gorgeous moment is “All I need Is The Girl” performed nearly solo by one of the young men in the troupe, Tulsa (Kevin Csolak).  Camille A. Brown created a stunning soft shoe solo to intermingle with the song, and the combination is so brilliant it nearly stops the show.

Kevin Csolak & Joy Woods – Photo by Julieta Cervantes

What does stop the show is McDonald’s “Rose’s Turn”.  This is where you realize that “Gypsy” is, at its core, a classic tale.  It is King Lear meets MacBeth.  We could not ask for a better tragic hero nor a better interpreter of Rose’s decent into a kind of lonely madness as the walls close in and the blinders have been removed.  A few of us (myself included) started whooping before the number was over (much to the chagrin of my guest) but we couldn’t help it.  McDonald’s specificity and willingness to let Rose pull out all the stops and tumble into her own personal disarray is nothing less than miraculous.

This Rose doesn’t travel alone.  She takes us into the dungeon of her passionate loneliness and drags us with her when she pulls herself back into the light out of sheer force of will – just like she has done everything else.

A nod to the score (Jule Styne and Stephen Sondheim).  It is astonishing how many of the songs have stood on their own and become part of the Great American Songboook: “Some People,” “Small World,” “You’ll Never Get Away From Me,” “All I Need Is The Girl.”  And that’s just the first act.

Let me be clear – theses actors are all giving 100%.  They are a HUGE gorgeous ensamble.  The gulf between them and McDonald, however, is a wide one that is constant theoughout.

And not for nothing, but in summer stock we came up with a way for Tessie Tura’s butterfly to flap it’s wings, one at a time and on cue.  No one figured that out here.  More’s the pity.  Somebody shoulda called me.

Just sayin’.

And PS the conductor, Andy Einhorn, althought he is never seen by the audience except by those of us who turn to find the video flatscreens mounted on the mezzanine rail – well this guy wears a tux jacket and a bowtie and conducts like he is part elft.  Quite excellent.

GYPSY is suggested by the memoirs of Gypsy Rose Lee. Directed by George C. Wolfe.  Book by Arthur Laurents, music by Jule Styne, and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim, choreography by Camille A. Brown

Scenic design by Santo Loquasto, costume design by Toni-Leslie James, lighting design by Jules Fisher + Peggy Eisenhauer, sound design by Scott Lehrer, hair and wig design by Mia Neal, makeup design by Michael Clifton.

WITH Audra McDonald, Danny Burstein, Joy Woods, Jordan Tyson, Kevin Csolak, Lesli Margherita, Lili Thomas, Mylinda Hull, Jacob Ming-Trent, Kyleigh Denae Vickers, Marley Lianne Gomes, Jade Smith, Natalie Wachen, Tryphena Wade, Shanel Bailey, Jace Bently, Brandon Burks, Hunter Capellán, Tony d’Alelio, Summer Rae Daney, Kellie Jean Hoagland, Sasha Hutchings, Aliah James, Brittney Johnson, Zachary Daniel Jones, Ethan Joseph, Andrew Kober, Krystal Mackie, James McMenamin, Cole Newburg, Joe Osheroff, Majo Rivero, Ken Robinson, Sally Shaw, Thomas Silcott, Brendan Sheehan, Jayden Theophile, Jordan Wynn and Iain Young.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Vahni Kurra

Amongst the offerings of this year’s Under the Radar festival, Mehr Theatre Group’s Blind Runner is not to be missed. Written and directed by Amir Reza Koohestani, a visionary in Iran’s contemporary theatre scene, Blind Runner is a rattling and devastating ride through incarceration, exile, and a marriage pushed to the brink. Currently playing at St. Ann’s Warehouse, the Brooklyn playhouse has created a fantastic, immersive experience for theatre-goers with a pre-show Persian tea room and art gallery featuring Iranian artists.

The play unfolds in a series of high tension visits, punctuated by moments of marital teasing, between a political prisoner (Ainaz Azarhoush) and her husband (Mohammed Reza Hosseinzadeh) in Tehran. At his wife’s insistence, the husband agrees to train and guide a young blind woman named Parissa (played again by Azarhoush) through a Parisian footrace. Their relationship becomes increasingly close, culminating in the blind runner asking her guide to embark with her on a deadly challenge: running the channel tunnel from France to England in just a few hours before the first morning train hits them.

The dialogue is in Farsi with English supertitles, giving a lifelike texture to the characters’ interactions. Although occasionally the timing between the actors’ dialogue and the supertitles were off, the supertitles operator (Negar Nobakht Foghani) does a good job of staying on top of the snappy lines exchanged by the two actors. Plus, the stage design helped immensely. Through an ingenious use of discrete cameras, realtime close-ups of the actors’ faces and superimposed images of their full bodies are projected at the back of the stage onto a domineering screen below the surtitles. This not only allows for more seamless viewing for those of us reliant on translations, but adds a new depth to the play’s themes and revelations.

Photo by Amir Hamja

The cameras make us aware that every minute movement or potentially subversive word is being monitored. Hosseinzadeh and Azarhoush’s dialogue and facial expressions carefully tiptoe through sensitive topics such as the likelihood of her being released early, whether they can speak freely, and what prison life is actually like. The natural exchange between Hosseinzadeh and Azarhoush is engrossing and potent, with the couple flipping quickly from witty teasing to barbed accusations about each other’s loyalty. They are masters of wielding vulnerability, betraying each other through verbal missteps and an inability for each character to truly understand the other’s experience. When the husband says he wants to be able to hold her hand and get her out, she tells him that is what people on the outside think. “And you who are on the inside, what are you like?” He asks with simmering resentment. “We know that false hopes are worse than despair,” she says simply.

In the moments between dialogue, the characters run in parallel beams of light that illuminate the stage floor. The runners are projected as superimposed videos on the large screen, creating a dreamlike state that only deepens as the prison sentence continues. Through the multifaceted staging, we see a portrait of two people whose lives are intimately connected, yet are forced to always be just out of reach, existing on parallel lines that never meet.

Trapped in prison, the wife’s world has shrunk from the open road where she and her husband ran races to a single corridor. It is an unfathomable mutilation of everyday life that could be reduced to stereotypes by another playwright, yet in Koohestani’s capable hands, he captures a quintessential experience in the struggle for freedom. To write the play, Koohestani relied on the interviews conducted by political prisoner Zia Nabavi, who talked to tens of thousands of prisoners about the different kind of life they led while incarcerated. This life is almost incomprehensible to people on the outside, and the toll it takes is portrayed in increasingly heartrending scenes that accelerate the play towards its high stakes, politically poignant ending. When the husband leaves to coach the blind runner, Parissa, the show moves more into a surreal imbalance where the husband and Parissa’s newly synced running rhythm becomes more regular as his marriage grows more off kilter. Together, Parissa and the husband enter a dangerous relationship that pushes both of them to risk the little physical security they have in order to bring justice to the political prisoners and asylum seekers of their home. With Koohestani’s exacting directing, the pace of the play is such that you never feel that there is a wasted moment. In the ongoing governmental crackdown on dissident expression and women’s bodily autonomy in Iran, Blind Runner is a vital scream in the struggle for a free society. See it before it’s gone!

—–

BLIND RUNNER – Written and Directed by Amir Reza Koohestani

WITH: Ainaz Azarhoush (Wife), Mohammed Reza Hosseinzadeh (Husband)

Dramaturgy by Samaneg Ahmadian; costumes and surtitles operation by Negar Nobakht Foghan; lights and scenography by Éric Soyer; video by Yasi Moradi, Benjamin Krieg; music by Phillip Hohenwarter, Matthias Peyker; production administration and promotion, Pierre Reiss; production video, St. Ann’s Warehouse, Julia Frey; production audio, St. Ann’s Warehouse, Alex Loving; lighting programmer, Bridget Chervenka; stage manager, Mithra Seyedi.

Presented in partnership with Waterwell and Nimruz, and part of Under the Radar.

At St. Ann’s Warehouse, 718-254-8779, stannswarehouse.org. Through January 24. Running time: 60 minutes. No intermission.

title.rendered: Handel’s Messiah, Presented at Carnegie Hall by the Oratorio Society of New York. Review by Betsyann Faiella

content.rendered:
By Betsyann Faiella

The Oratorio Society of New York (est. 1873) presented its 150th holiday performance of Handel’s Messiah on Dec. 23rd at Stern Auditorium / Perelman Stage at Carnegie Hall. “The Messiah,” however, has been around since 1742, when George Frideric Handel composed the nearly three-hour work in 24 days, anticipating a charity event in Dublin.

The impressive program was led by Conductor Kent Tritle, and featured, naturally, the Oratorio Chorus and the Oratorio Orchestra. Mr. Tritle has a very serious pedigree, and his skill, sensitivity and enthusiasm were on display as he led the singers and musicians.

Messiah is a narrative of the history of Jesus Christ in three parts. So if you don’t want to come for the story, come for the skill and artistry. The first part prophesies the birth, the second pays homage to his sacrifice for mankind, and the final section celebrates his resurrection.

It’s interesting to read the various histories of Handel. Apparently he died a wealthy man, but at the time he was composing the Messiah oratorio, he was dead broke. And then, the Messiah didn’t actually catch on immediately, but its popularity grew with time.

The soloists were Soprano Nola Richardson, Countertenor Aryeh Nussbaum Cohen, Tenor Joshua Blue, and Bass-baritone Joseph Parrish. My enjoyment of these singers varied, with the standout being the countertenor, Cohen, whose pitch was perfect and every word distinguishable.

This oratorio of Handel’s was, apparently, different than other oratorios, in that the chorus propels the work forward. There are no “characters” presented in this work like other oratorios. It is simply sung, and though there are recitatives, there is no purely spoken word. The libretto was fashioned by Handel’s friend, Charles Jennens, and Handel from Old Testament scripture. The phrases are repeated and varied many times by soloists or chorus, and the effect is very exciting.

The chorus performed beautifully. It was robust and pitch- perfect always. The soloists were, it appeared, only mic-ed by one instrument from above, and though it’s Carnegie Hall and acoustics are sublime, I felt they might have benefited from just a bit more amplification.

I had trouble with the Tenor, Joshua Blue, whose vibrato was so extreme that he was pitchy. In fact, with the exception of the Countertenor Cohen, the soloists all sang with extreme vibrato, (with a little less from the Bass-Baritone, Parrish). Extreme vibrato is not my favorite frequency.

Nonetheless, the evening was a beautiful Christmas and Holiday Season outing.

There is a story about the origin of the tradition of standing during the Hallelujah Chorus. It is said that King George II rose from his seat at this point. Some say it was to pay homage to the beauty of the work. Others say it was to honor Jesus Christ, the King of Kings. These stories and more are contested vociferously online! But my favorite retort to the many comments I’ve read is this:

“If you want to stand because it moves you, then you should stand. I think that’s good, because people are yearning to do things together, to celebrate things together. So if standing during the Hallelujah chorus offers you that experience, go for it.’’

Handel’s Messiah presented at Carnegie Hall by the Oratorio Society of New York. Dec. 23, 2024 at 7PM. Isaac Stern Auditorium /Ronald O. Perelman Stage. Kent Tritle, Conductor. Nola Richardson, Soprano. Aryeh Nussbaum Cohen, Countertenor. Joshua Blue, Tenor. Joseph Parrish, Bass-Baritone.
Photo: Brian Hatton

title.rendered: Betty Gilpin to Replace Cole Escola joined by Phillip James Brannon and Chris Renfro

content.rendered:
The Broadway comedy “Oh, Mary!” will welcome a new title player. Three-time Emmy Award nominee Betty Gilpin will take over the role of Mary Todd Lincoln for an eight-week limited engagement from Jan. 21 through March 16, 2025. Gilpin will succeed playwright Cole Escola, who will exit the comedy at the Lyceum Theatre on Jan. 19.

She’ll be joined by the newly announced Phillip James Brannon (Macbeth), succeeding Conrad Ricamora as Mary’s Husband; and Chris Renfro (Queer as Folk), succeeding James Scully as Mary’s Teacher.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: Classics for Christmas: Mozart, Bach, and Beethoven Illuminate Carnegie Hall

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

The timeless allure of Carnegie Hall set the stage for an unforgettable evening on December 18, as Musica Sacra, under the brilliant direction of maestro Kent Tritle, delivered a breathtaking concert entitled Classics for Christmas: Mozart, Bach, and Beethoven. The evening masterfully intertwined the jubilance of the season with the profundity of timeless choral and orchestral works, reaffirming Musica Sacra’s place as a beacon of musical excellence.

Maestro Kent Tritle. Photo by Jennifer Taylor

An Intimate Encounter in Carnegie Hall

Carnegie Hall’s legendary acoustics cradled every note, making each sound feel personal and profound. The historic venue’s walls, steeped in the echoes of past maestros, seemed to embrace the Musica Sacra Chorus and Orchestra as they began Bach’s Christmas Oratorio. From the opening subtle expressive content of “Jauchzet, frohlocket, auf, preiset die Tage,” the audience was captivated. With its bright virtuosic trumpets, rich orchestral strains, and choral crystalline purity, this joyous piece with its exquisite joinings heralded the Christmas spirit.

The experience of sitting among an enraptured full house was divine. Carnegie Hall’s grandeur and intimacy blended seamlessly with the evening’s effulgent repertoire, creating an organic connection between performer and listener.

The Genius of Kent Tritle

Kent Tritle’s reputation as one of the world’s foremost choral conductors was evident throughout the performance. Known for his precise, expressive direction and inspired interpretations, Tritle shaped each piece into a tapestry of sound rich in emotional depth. His meticulous attention to detail revealed the joyous interplay between the orchestra and chorus, particularly in Bach’s exuberant trumpet passages.

Tritle’s leadership style exudes warmth and inspiration, fostering an environment where each musician’s talent shines. Under his guidance, Musica Sacra’s cohesive artistry elevated the evening to a higher plane.

Bach’s Sublime Christmas Oratorio

Bach’s Christmas Oratorio is a masterpiece that encapsulates the nativity story’s joy, ebullience, and reverence. Tritle’s direction ensured that every nuance was brought to life. In “Briocht an, o schönes Morgenlicht,” the shimmering chorale unfolded with angelic purity, while “Ach, mein herzliebes Jesulein” was tenderly introspective, inviting the audience into the intimate cradle of Bethlehem.

The famously demanding piccolo trumpet parts were executed flawlessly, adding jubilant brilliance to the performance. The balance between orchestra and chorus was superb, a testament to Tritle’s skillful leadership.

Johann Sebastian Bach (aged 61) in a portrait by Elias Gottlob Haussmann, the second version of his 1746 canvas. Public Domain

Francis Poulenc and Morten Lauridsen: Modern Reflections

Francis Poulenc’s a cappella Hodie Christus natus est was a revelation. The chorus’s crisp articulation and refined musicality imbued the work with jubilant energy and showcased their extraordinary vocal precision.

Lauridsen’s O Magnum Mysterium followed, enveloping the hall in a meditative stillness. This modern choral gem explores the mystery of Christ’s birth with lush chromatic and close harmonies with pensive, ethereal textures. Musica Sacra’s performance highlighted the exquisite interplay of light and shadow within the piece, leaving the audience spellbound.

Mozart’s Exultate, Jubilate with Susanna Phillips

With unmatched artistry, Soprano Susanna Phillips brought Mozart’s Exultate, Jubilate to life. Her melismatic passages in the “Exultate jubilate” movement flowed effortlessly, capturing the piece’s joyful exuberance. In the recitative “Fulget amica dies,” Phillips delivered each phrase with exquisite, expressive clarity, seamlessly transitioning to the climactic “Alleluia.”

Her radiant and agile voice was a highlight of the evening, earning her rapturous ovations. Phillips’ ability to convey heartfelt emotion with technical brilliance affirmed her place among today’s premier sopranos. Phillips’s masterful melismatic passages were dazzlingly radiant.

Susann Phillips, Soprano. Courtesy susannaphillips.com

James Bassi and Franz Biebl: Hidden Gems

The a cappella rendering of James Bassi’s Quem pastores laudavere demonstrated the ensemble’s dynamic range and emotional depth. This tender piece unfolded with introspective beauty, its chromaticism accentuated by the chorus’s seamless blend.

Franz Biebl’s Ave Maria offered a moment of profound serenity. The interplay between the soloists and chorus created a prayerful atmosphere, with each phrase resonating deeply in the hearts of the listeners.

Beethoven’s Choral Fantasy: A Grand Finale

The evening concluded with Beethoven’s monumental Choral Fantasy, Op. 80. This work, often regarded as a precursor to his Ninth Symphony, brought all the performers together in a triumphant culmination. Pianist Simone Dinnerstein’s virtuosity was mesmerizing as she navigated the demanding piano introduction with dramatic flair and precision.

The vocal soloists, including sopranos Susanna Phillips and Elizabeth van Os, Countertenor Jonathan May, Tenors Chad Kranak and John Kawa, and Baritone Harrison Hintzche, delivered a rousing performance of depth, confidence, brilliance, and power. Their voices soared above the orchestra, blending harmoniously with the chorus and resonating with the sonic richness of the finest pipe organ.

Dinnerstein’s mastery and the ensemble’s synergy captured Beethoven’s vision of unity and celebration, leaving the audience in awe.

Simone Dinnerstein, Pianist. Courtesy simonedinnerstein.com

Why Musica Sacra Shines Bright

Musica Sacra, New York’s longest-continuously performing professional chorus, has a storied history of excellence. Under Kent Tritle’s leadership, the ensemble has reached new artistic heights, presenting programs that blend tradition with innovation.

Their dedication to musical precision and emotional resonance ensures that each performance is a transformative experience. The Classics for Christmas concert exemplified their commitment to bringing timeless works to life with fresh vitality.

A Celebration of Christmas and Community

This concert was more than a showcase of technical brilliance; it was a heartfelt celebration of the Christmas season. Each piece, from Bach’s jubilant chorales to Beethoven’s triumphant finale, conveyed hope, joy, and unity.

Musica Sacra’s ability to connect with audiences on such a profound level is a testament to their artistry and passion. Their music transcends boundaries, reminding us of the universal power of song to uplift and inspire.

Plan Your Next Musica Sacra Experience

For those who missed this extraordinary evening, Musica Sacra’s upcoming concerts promise more opportunities to experience the irresistible pulchritude of their musical delectations. Check your calendars and visit their official website.

Final Words

The Classics for Christmas concert was a magnificent journey through the finest choral music, performed with unparalleled artistry. Musica Sacra and Kent Tritle continue to enrich our cultural landscape, offering moments of beauty and reflection that resonate long after the final note. This concert was not just a performance but a celebration of music’s power to unite, inspire, and transform.

Bravo!

Classics for Christmas: Mozart, Bach, and Beethoven Illuminate Carnegie Hall

Musica Sacra

Kent Tritle, music director/conductor
https://kenttritle.com
Kent Tritle on Facebook: www.facebook.com/kenttritle
Kent Tritle on Twitter: www.twitter.com/kenttritle
Join Kent Tritle’s e-newsletter list.

For information and tickets, go to https://musicasacrany.com/

Readers may also enjoy Oratorio Society of New York with Bach’s Magnificat and Mozart’s Requiem, Magical Christmas in New York: 20 Best Activities, and Mozart’s Ave Verum Corpus: A Perfect Sacred Miniature.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Leslye Headland‘s latest play, Cult of Love, now playing at Broadway’s Helen Hayes Theater, is the final one in her cycle of plays about the seven deadly sins. This one touches on pride and how by dogmatically sticking to it, one becomes blinded to the world around them.

Despite the cloaked slings and arrows the Dahl family constantly fling at one another, the journey of this play has much to offer in the way of upper-middle-class family dynamics, personal growth, tolerance, and the ties that bind despite the whirling winds. You’ll get to say, “At least my family isn’t as bad as that,” and laugh at the blind inconsiderateness disguised as loving care.

A lot is covered here and it all doesn’t get fleshed out, but that’s okay. Life doesn’t give us pat answers to all of our questions and dilemmas, but what it does give us is a journey that we have to take alone. The scariness of that aloneness brings us to search for understanding and companionship which is not always the best thing for us.

The Dahl parents (Mare Winningham and David Rasche) both came from lives of great dysfunction lacking love and the fear of not knowing what was going to happen next. They made a pact that they were not going to repeat and created a family that was insular and flooded with oppressive love (the Dahl cult). Even though their kids are now grown and out on their own, they still fight that fight from their childhood trying to keep the world at bay.

What that gives us of course, is a dysfunctional family Christmas special replete with the, “You refuse to accept my lifestyle” child (Rebecca Henderson), the “lost” child trying to pretend that they have it all together (Zachary Quinto), the recovering drug/alcohol child (Christopher Sears), and the child that has always been too sensitive, physically and emotionally, and has always needed a little more attention than the rest (Shailene Woodley).

It’s Christmas Eve in a lovely old Connecticut family home decorated up for the holidays like a Thomas Kinkade card (another great set by John Lee Beatty). The snow continually flutters outside the window and the Dahl family has assembled for the yearly get-together. It’s a family where the only way they can stay in harmony with one another is by playing music and singing. But once the final note sounds and the voices fade, the fires burning behind their personal walls flare up again.

The Christmas songs that they sing to pull them out of their pain and find connection are accompanied by piano, banjo, ukelele, melodica, harmonica, washboard, and bells (a very talented Osmond-like family), are an actual delight and a welcome respite through the course of the evening from the emotional harm that they are continually inflicting upon each other. But this distraction of music can only do so much to keep the family’s inner fires at bay: aging, disappointment in self and others, anger and jealousy at that disappointment, and fear of what’s to come. A delightful time (tongue in cheek) is had by all both on the stage and in the audience.

—–

Written by: Leslye Headland
Director: Trip Cullman

Cast: Shailene Woodley (as Diana Dahl Bennett), Zachary Quinto (as Mark Dahl), Barbie Ferreira (as Loren Montgomery), Molly Bernard (as Rachel Dahl), Roberta Colindrez (as Pippa Ferguson), Rebecca Henderson (as Evie Dahl), Christopher Lowell (as James Bennett), Christopher Sears (as Johnny Dahl), Mare Winningham (as Ginny Dahl), David Rasche (as Bill Dahl)

Sets: John Lee Beatty
Costumes: Sophia Choi
Lighting: Heather Gilbert
Sound: Darron L West
Other info: Hair and makeup design by Liz Printz, music supervision by Jacinth Greywoode, dramaturgy by Eleanor Skimin

Hayes Theater 240 West 44th Street, New York, NY, 10036

Cult of Love runs for 1hr 45min. No intermission.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

When I was in fifth grade my class was assigned Pen Pals who lived in England and were students from a town with the same name as ours.  Once I got over the shock of the fact that there WAS another town with the same name, I got right to it.  We exchanged a few letters, and that was that.  I don’t recall what happened to my Pen Pal. I don’t remember her name or much of anything about her – except this: we were strangers connected.  In 1960 or so, this was a big deal.  In those days the only way we could communicate with people was through letters or telegrams in an emergency.  Long distance phone calls were within the country and expensive.

Letter writing was the deal.

It still is in “Pen Pals”.  Michael Griffo has created an intimate and delicate world between Bernadette Patricia O’Brien from Newark and Margaret Mary Marsch from Sheffield, England.  Known henceforward as Bernie and Mags.  Their story begins in the fall of 1955 when both are 14-ish years old.  Both are filled with thoughts and few people to share them with.  

These are iconic young women with what we might call the typical childhoods if you think of the world as white middle class.  Rock Hudson was a dreamboat and Natalie Wood was the envy of every teenage girl.  In some ways this works, because the teenage years back in the 1950’s and early 1960’s were self centered on the surface until the social movements of Civil Rights and the Vietnam War exploded into our living rooms.  And, oh yeah, the Beatles.

Griffo prefers to stay on the safe side and stick to these girls’ romantic relationships.  Not entirely safe, mind you.  Issues of intercourse, abortion, fetal death, aging parents and a wide variety of diseases are presented with no gift wrapping.  Love, marriage, motherhood and true love are weighed and picked over.  What is not discussed is the volatile world these two lived in.  Their friendship spans 50 years for goodness sakes. 1955-2005.  What about The John Kennedy assassination?  The March on Washington.  Deaths of RFK and MLK.  Feminism?  Princess Diana?  Aids.  Legalization of gay marriage?  The moonlanding. Any of these would have been rich topics for discussion.

And finally – why limit them to mail when the price of airline trips was plummeting?  These two women deserved to put their feet up in front of the same cozy fireplace.   And we would have loved to listen to that conversation.

It is a rich tapestry – that is for certain – one that has us rooting for them from the start.  Wished that we had been allowed to go a bit deeper where more is always at stake.

With a rotating cast starting with Johanna Day and Nancy McKeon – you have your pick!

Pen Pals Written by Michael Griffo and Directed by SuzAnne Barabas

WITH Johanna Day and Nancy McKeon through December 22.  Rotating cast to follow through February 9.

Design by Jessica Parks, costume design by David C. Woolard, lighting design by Jill Nagle, sound design by Nick Simone.  In association with NJ Repertory Company.

Pen Pals is proud to partner with the Susan G. Komen® and will donate 5% of the total ticket sales and 100% of all customer donations collected to Susan G. Komen®, whose mission is to save lives by meeting the most critical needs in our communities and investing in breakthrough research to prevent and cure breast cancer.

Tickets HERE

Theatre at St. Clements 423 W 46th St, New York, NY 10036

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: T.3 Delights at City Winery NYC: A Holiday Tour Worth Singing About

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

Cabaret Magic in the Heart of Manhattan

Step into City Winery on a December night, and the atmosphere feels downright enchanted. It’s intimate, electric, and pulsing with the sounds of holiday cheer. Nestled in a snug corner of Manhattan’s vibrant arts scene, City Winery evokes a vintage cabaret energy. Think candlelit tables, clinking glasses, and a velvet-draped backstage — perfect for a trio like T.3 to shine.

Warming up the crowd before T.3. was the a capella group Blackout. Check them out. We’ll be hearing a lot more from them!

The venue, buzzing with an eager crowd, becomes a portal to simpler, joyful times. Fans laugh, sip their drinks, and eagerly anticipate what’s to come. Moments later, the spotlight hits, and out strolls three theater-seasoned performers — Liam Fennecken, Jim Hogan, and Brendan Jacob Smith. This is no ordinary show. This is T.3’s FaLaLaLonely tour, and it’s everything the season promised and more.

From Broadway Stages to Viral Stardom

T.3 is more than a trio of polished voices; they’re a phenomenon. Since wowing America’s Got Talent audiences in Season 16 with Into the Unknown, they’ve been on a fast track to national acclaim. That viral moment earned them over 4.6 million YouTube views, but the charm was always organic. Blending Broadway backgrounds with millennial sensibilities, they connect deeply with theater aficionados and TikTok-savvy fans.

Individually, their resumes speak volumes. In Kimberly Akimbo’s national tour, Jim Hogan exudes rich baritone brilliance. Liam Fennecken, fresh from Chicago as Amos Hart, brings warmth and charisma. Brendan Jacob Smith? The soulful storyteller. As Art Garfunkel in The Simon and Garfunkel Story, he effortlessly channels legends. Together, though, they transcend any solo credits.

FaLaLaLonely: An Evening of Musical Triumphs

This holiday season, T.3’s FaLaLaLonely is the gift we didn’t know we needed. In New York, they wrapped audiences in soaring harmonies and resonated storytelling. The show opened with the title track, FaLaLaLonely, a catchy, feel-good,  joyful, and merry tune. It’s the original song that sneaks into your playlist and never leaves.

Then came the covers. And oh, what covers they were. Disney magic arrived early with a soaring Let It Go, delivered with emotional precision. O Holy Night followed, a performance so lush it felt celestial. For Beach Boys fans, Little Saint Nick was reimagined, buoyed by Joshua Lee Turner’s collaboration, offering just the right splash of retro joy.

Mid-show, the trio slowed things down with Stevie Wonder’s Someday at Christmas. It was poignant, smooth, and offered a moment of reflection amid the festivity. The medley of mistletoe classics proved another highlight, with Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas stealing hearts.

Of course, T.3 knows its audience well. Broadway standards like Defying Gravity from Wicked and The Sound of Music medley drew a knowing cheer. My Favorite Things and Edelweiss shimmered with nostalgia. Yet, their cover of Kansas’ Carry On Wayward Son blew the roof off. Patrons clapped, sang, and rose to their feet — the energy was undeniable.

Original music also took center stage. Brendan Jacob Smith’s When I Knew You showcased introspection and heartfelt storytelling. It’s a testament to T.3’s artistry: They’re equally magnetic, delivering stripped-down originals as they are with powerhouse covers.

The Band and the Blend: Perfect Harmony

While T.3’s voices often steal the show, their backing band deserves equal praise. On drums, Josh Roberts drove rhythms with effortless dynamism. Damon Smith’s (Brendan Jacob Smith’s brother) keys added texture and drama, perfectly timed with David Kawamura’s brilliant, tasty lead guitar work. Meanwhile, Sean Muzzi’s bass grounded every number with subtle brilliance. Together, the instrumentalists elevated T.3’s arrangements into something transcendent.

Yet it always comes back to the voices. T.3’s harmonies remain their signature magic. They’re pitch-perfect, emotive, and sophisticated, effortlessly weaving vocal tapestries that make audiences swoon. Whether belting out O Holy Night or crooning Baby Please Come Home, their balance of power and intimacy is unmatched.

The T.3 Phenomenon: A Love That Spans Generations

T.3’s music possesses a universal appeal. Perhaps it’s the way they honor timeless classics while bringing contemporary flair. Or maybe it’s their playful online presence. With over 459k TikTok followers, they’ve proven a cappella is cool again. Fans adore their imaginative vocal takes and natural chemistry, making every performance feel personal. Besides, everyone enjoyed how the trio shared their holiday memories.

Their debut EP, Option Up, released in collaboration with Straight No Chaser’s SNC Records, cemented their place in the a cappella world. Featuring Broadway legends like Shoshana Bean and Morgan James, it was a masterclass in creative arrangements. Now, FaLaLaLonely extends that promise, delivering holiday cheer with tradition and originality.

The Future Sounds Bright for T.3

City Winery was just one stop on their ambitious 11-city holiday tour. From New York to Boston, Philadelphia to beyond, T.3 proves they’re more than a viral sensation. Their energy, craft, and love for music unite audiences, old and young alike.

T.3 is on stage at City Winery NYC for their national holiday tour. Photo by Edward Kliszus

For those yet to experience them live, don’t wait. T.3’s shows are electrifying, heartwarming, and utterly unforgettable. Their recordings — whether the soaring FaLaLaLonely or their take on Little Saint Nick — demand repeat listens. Stream their EPs, share their videos, and spread the word.

Why T.3 Deserves Your Attention

In a world awash with overproduced music, T.3’s artistry feels refreshingly authentic. Their voices, harmonies, and charisma leave audiences smiling, dancing, and occasionally wiping away tears. They’re proof that vocal precision, paired with genuine joy, transcends genres and generations.

This holiday season, let T.3’s FaLaLaLonely brighten your days. Whether live at a club or through a streaming service, their music promises something timeless and authentic. And as the audience at City Winery can attest, T.3 isn’t just another group. They’re a musical experience you don’t want to miss.

Catch T.3 on their holiday tour, stream their new EP FaLaLaLonely, and let their harmonies soundtrack your season.
